speechtext: Mr. Speaker, when I made a few remarks the other evening following immediately on the speech of the minister I began by saying that I doubted if the minister had enjoyed delivering his speech as much as he had the previous one. Now that I have had a better chance to study the budget speech I am inclined to think that that was a gross understatement. subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It is a difficult speech to criticize, because after all it is

The Budget-Mr. J. M. Macdonnell merely a kind of mixture of toilet soap and ice cream, which provides a most slippery surface from which to launch an attack. In some ways I find it something like trying to make a dent in a rubber ball.
That view was very widely held at the outset. Many hon. members may have seen the cartoon which appeared in the Globe and Mail. Incidentally I hope the minister has a scrapbook for these various cartoons, because I feel sure they would prove most interesting for his descendants. This cartoon depicts the minister as a small figure, but I think the artist has done well by him; the picture shows that mixture of good humour and earnestness with which we are familiar. The minister is shown as being mounted on the back of a big elephant, and the cartoon is entitled "The Budget Parade". One sees the people looking on, and one gentleman is rushing up to see the minister, who unfortunately has just gone by on the big elephant. As this gentleman is wearing a tail coat, I assume that the artist intended to depict him as a large tax payer. A policeman is holding up his hand to hold him back, and is saying, "You didn't miss a thing; you saw it all last year".
I suppose there is a certain virtue in that. Last year I saw a cartoon depicting the minister as a gunman, and I suppose there are many other ways in which he has been depicted. I hope that one day he will be depicted as the undertaker of the Liberal party.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: No chance of that.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
At first there was a disposition to pooh-pooh this budget speech, as if it did not amount to much; but on second thought people had a different feeling. In spite of the negative quality of the speech, or perhaps because of it, I think people have come to feel that the speech is worthy of serious attention. Let us look at the story which it tells.
Hon. members will recall that last year the minister was able to give tax reductions of $323 million, although we were quick to point out that that was just election pump-priming. Nevertheless the reduction was given, and of course the people liked to get it. The saints liked to get it, just as much as the sinners; everybody liked to get it. As the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Cruickshank) would say if he were here, and as he did say the other night, it did a good election job.
Now we come to grips with the figures for this year. There is an estimated revenue of $2,430 million and estimated expenditures of $2,410 million, giving a surplus of $20 million.

Twenty. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) I think is unrivalled in his knowledge of the rules of the house, but apparently his arithmetic is not quite so good. I agree that it is a microscopic surplus which might disappear at any time the minister is not looking. I doubt if the minister thinks much of it himself, because he used rather doleful words about the situation. The minister told us plainly that we must "cope somehow"-I call your attention to the word "somehow"- "with a continuing level of expenditure of $2,400 million, even in the absence of large-scale economic difficulties or widespread unemployment." I take it these last phrases mean that we must spend that amount even if times are good. Even if there is no special drain on us the best we can hope for is $2,400 million. Of course if there were unemployment or economic difficulties, presumably that figure would increase and the $20 million would be gone before you could say "knife".
It is true that the minister adds-I quote from Hansard at page 1215:
Naturally we hope to reduce expenditures by improved efficiency in operation, and by economies in administration.
The minister is a rather cheerful chap. In spite of an obviously gloomy budget, the cheerfulness breaks in from time to time; but in the next minute he is uttering another dirge and he warns us that:
It is only by reducing government activities or social security payments that any major reductions can be made.
I think as we go on we may find that is only too true. At any rate, it is only too true so long as the present attitude of the government remains. There is not much inspiration in that. There is not much sense of urgency. There is no real suggestion that this problem is going to be attacked. The minister seems to be on the defensive, and perhaps it would not be unfair to add that there is a little note of defeatism in what he says. He rather underlined that note of defeatism; and later we find that the minister says again:
But we should not delude ourselves with the belief that we can significantly alter the scale of the budget in this way.
By the phrase "in this way" he means by making economies. It is only fair to say that we have had, as the minister points out, a substantial increase in defence and social security services, and one would be unfair enough not to recognize the burden which the minister has had to carry.
Finally we come to something in the minister's speech which really sounds to me like a signal of distress. He says, at page 1216:
Unless we are prepared to reduce the scope or scale of government activities, we must now expect $2,400 million budgets in future years. Nor can we

escape the tax implications of this conclusion. We must have a tax system that will at least balance the budget in good years . . .
I will draw your attention to that again in a moment.
.	.	. otherwise we should slide quickly into
inflation.
Remember again that we are told, and I think correctly, that 1949 was a good year. The estimate of the gross national income for the current year, if I remember correctly, is $300 million above 1949, which itself was $500 million above 1948. Therefore it is forecast as a big year. We have now come a long way from the "substantial surpluses" which the minister assured us not so long ago should be characteristic of good years so as to prepare for years not so good. In other words, the best that can be said, even in this year that we expect will be good, is that if unemployment does not rise too much and trade does not go down too much we may break even. If that is the best in good times, then what about bad times? The minister does not mention that, but I think it is a reasonable question to ask, and I think we can answer it for ourselves. I think every reasonable person expects that expenditures will have to go up, and will go up, unless very drastic economies can be made; because, after all, does anyone believe that the government can squirm out of all its social security promises? Surely something will have to be done there, and surely that will lead us into a deficit unless one of two things happens: either we bring down our expenses substantially, or we are able to raise our income substantially.
In other words, in this period of high prosperity the minister has very little comfort to give us. If there is any setback, we have a deficit. We can really go further and say, as I said a moment ago, that it is extremely hard to believe that increases in expenditure will not take place. Without economies or increased output we will certainly have a deficit or increased taxation. We should be grateful to the minister for his candour. He certainly has given us fair warning, but we do not need to follow him in what I have called defeatism. I am not primarily interested in trying to criticize the minister. What I want to do is to try to get at what seems to be the reality of the situation. The minister's picture is grave enough, although, as I said, cheerfulness breaks through and occasionally distracts us from the seriousness of what he said.
In order to try to make this simple, real, and everyday, I should like to picture the situation in terms of the life of the ordinary man, and, let us say, of a co-operative. I would say that our financial position,
4, 1950
The Budget-Mr. J. M. Macdonnell expressed in terms of the affairs of an ordinary individual, is like that of a person who has had an unexpectedly large income for some years. He has been able to pay off some debts, but he is now living right up to his income, and unless his income remains at that level he has no right to expect he must look forward to anything except a shortage.
Let me now give the illustration of a cooperative of which all citizens are members. All active citizens contribute and they all receive services. In good years they hope to get dividends also; in other words, a rebate on their payments. They have been told that the coming year will be a good year, like other years in which they sometimes have had dividends. They hoped at the worst to break even, but they now find that their contributions in the coming year at the very best will enable them to break even, and may easily do worse than that. They have been told that expenditures cannot come down, and they believe it is quite likely that expenditures will go up and income will come down. In those circumstances they will face either a deficit or an additional levy. The only hope of avoiding this is, on the one hand, a substantial reduction of expenditures, or, on the other hand, a substantial increase in income.
I need not point the moral of this in terms of our own national life. I need not labour the point. I have suggested that today citizens of Canada are like members of a co-operative, and that they face the difficulty which I have endeavoured to describe. In passing let me say that, whereas the minister has naturally been proud to tell us in the past about payments made in reduction of the debt, payment on the debt this year makes a very small and insignificant story. If I read the figures correctly, we have paid off some $497 million, but of that amount only $67 million came from income. The rest came from realization of capital assets.
This situation would be serious enough if we were operating at a moderate level and with plenty of room for expansion, but at the present moment there seems to be nothing to warrant that. There is no particular reason to think that our trade will improve; on the contrary there is a good deal of reason to think that the present shrinkage will continue. I shall have more to say about that later.
I should also like to point out that the attitude of the government towards trade- and I am quite sure that our trade commissioners have been doing their best and all that sort of thing-has been negative, barren and un-co-operative. They are just hoping and waiting for something to turn up.

The Budget-Mr. J. M. Macdonnell As I said, anyone who expects the present high level oi trade to remain undisturbed is really doing the ostrich act. I propose to say something about that later, and particularly about what I regard as the antediluvian method we follow in this house in dealing with our accounts.
I want to say a word about trade. There is widespread uneasiness about trade. Last Friday the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) gave us a picture in which he painted practically a new heaven and a new earth; nevertheless there is widespread uneasiness, and before going further with the budget I should like to give a few facts and then make one or two comments on what the minister stated last Friday.
Our domestic exports since August of last year have shown a tendency to decline. I do not propose to detain the house with many figures, but I would like to give the figures for the months since then, showing our domestic exports to all countries, excluding gold:

It will be noted that in December, 1949, the trend was reversed, no doubt because of some special reasons about which the minister could tell us. However, those figures show the trend since last August.
I want to digress for a moment to say a word on what the minister said about Marshall aid. He rather pooh-poohed it, and I think it worth while to remind the house of the figures and of the great help it has been to us in the past, because we cannot face the future intelligently without knowing what has come to us through Marshall aid in the past. The total amount of Marshall aid in 1948 and 1949 was $7,850 million, of which $1,036 million was earmarked for Canada, and for Canada and the United States altogether, $6,527 million. While only $1,036 million was earmarked for Canada, that does not give the full extent of the effect of this aid, because, after all, the large dollar advances which other countries obtained under Marshall aid would certainly set free other dollar resources which they possessed; so it is perfectly reasonable to assume that the benefit we obtained from Marshall aid was far in excess of the amount actually earmarked for us.
I should like to direct attention briefly to what seem to be one or two essential features
(Mr. Macdonnell (Greenwood).]

of the trade situation in the last few years. In 1947 two significant events took place: first, the Geneva trade agreement was concluded; second, the attempt to make the British pound convertible at $4.03 failed, and of course that failure had a devastating effect upon the Geneva agreement. That agreement, as we all remember, had escape clauses under which nations could withhold the tariff advantages they had agreed to give if in fact their balance of payments was out of scale. In plain words this means that as a result of foreign exchange control and the turmoil of the exchanges, the nations were forced into the position where, with the exception of the United States, they very largely departed from the terms of the agreement, which became more or less inoperative. It was a frustrated effort.
From the point of view of tariff negotiators the Geneva agreement was a dream. They got tariffs down below where they had been for a generation; but the paralysing hand of controls came down upon them and spoiled the effect.
There were other escape clauses of an entirely different nature whereby nations could suspend the operation of the agreement if their own industries were going to be injured. This has been important only in the case of the United States, where there have been six such applications. Five of these have been turned down. The sixth, concerning aluminum, is now under consideration. I understand the board which reviews these applications is strictly political, being composed of three Democrats and three Republicans. Therefore I think we may have a good deal of hope that this application will be turned down also, because there will be no majority in favour of giving effect to the request. In the case of the United Kingdom, where tariffs were low and tariff reductions were not really matters of importance, their place was taken with unhappy effectiveness by import regulations of all kinds, so in that way the United Kingdom has made use of balance of payment difficulties to escape the effects which otherwise would have followed.
Now I should like to point out, in fact to repeat, that if in 1947 our financial experts had been able to do as satisfactory a job as our tariff experts, we would have had a very different situation. We know what has happened. We know they were not able to do that satisfactory job. We know what has been the turmoil of the exchanges since that time. We know that just the other day we were notified that the United Kingdom is cutting back its purchases by some twenty-six per cent, I think it is, which I am informed

is the result of the discussions and negotiations that took place last year, to which the minister referred.
I spoke of the turmoil of the exchanges. I spoke of the devaluation last autumn, to which the minister has also referred. Britain has made progress since then. Apparently it has been able to increase its exports to this country so that they earn the same amount of dollars they did before. Hon. members will bear in mind, of course, that with the pound depreciated the British have to export just that much more goods in order to get the same amount of dollars. But in spite of their progress he would be a bold man who would today predict that before the end of Marshall aid they will be able to span the gap, which is already large. I believe there is only one solution to the problem which offers any hope. It is a solution I have put to this house before; that is, a move toward the freeing of the exchanges. I have no intention of repeating my speech on exchange control, but what is happening every day in my view underlines the position we in this party have taken.
Let us see what is happening. In his speech last week the minister said at page 1208:
... it already seems clear that the action we took in September last has, under the conditions now prevailing, improved our trading position.
Well, I mention in passing that this hardly seems to square with the figures I gave a few moments ago, but the minister might reply by saying that if it had not been for what they did last September things might have been worse. Then let us see what has happened since last September. On the 19th of that month the minister said, as reported at page 56 of Hansard, second session, 1949:
For some time it has been clear that a fairly radical realignment of some currencies was a necessary element in the readjustments required to balance international trade.
The minister is certainly right. That had been clear, except for those people whose hands and minds were fast in strait-jackets. We all remember the case of Cripps, the British chancellor of the exchequer, who kept repeating that he would not and could not devalue, and then of course had to do it; like the old saw, "saying he would ne'er consent, consented." We can sympathize with him, moving from one crisis to another because of his fanatical adherence to the system of controls and his apparent unwillingness to take any step away from them.
On September 19-and I think this is important-referring to the discussion he had had with the United Kingdom and the United States the minister said, again at page 56:
Each of the participants was keenly and deeply aware of the consequences of failure. Unless the trend could be reversed, the free world would,
The Budget-Mr. J. M. Macdonnell through the force of events, divide itself into two economic blocs. With this division there could not be a sound or lasting basis for political co-operation and security.
I think we will all agree with that. Let us see what has happened. As I told you a few minutes ago, the minister says the situation has improved. That, however, seems to me to be a doubtful proposition. Let us call the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) to give evidence on that point as to whether these blocs are becoming less sharply defined. Speaking after his return from Colombo, as reported at page 135 of Hansard of February 22, the minister said they had
. . . highly qualified experts at these talks.
Further on he says:
They-
That is, the talks.
-concerned in the main the present position and future prospects of the sterling area. The Canadian position with respect to participation in talks of this kind was, if I may say so, a little equivocal.
I was surprised at that word "equivocal". I looked it up to see what the dictionary had to say about it; and it says, "capable of double interpretation." There are those in this house who would say that things of that kind have been said by this government, capable of double or perhaps even triple interpretations. But I do not think this was one of them because I think, as a matter of fact, the minister's attitude was only too clear, and I quote again from what he said. He says:
It-
That is, the Canadian position.
-certainly was not the same as that of the other participating representatives, who, without exception, came from the sterling areas. In fact our role at those talks, if I may put it that way, was that of a persistent but very friendly dollar gadfly.
In other words, our only objective was to sting others into action but apparently not to do much ourselves. That point became underlined when an amendment was moved in this house suggesting a commonwealth conference and when the Minister of Finance, while not saying that the conference might not be of value, and while saying that if we were invited we would of course go, nevertheless was not prepared to take any initiative in summoning it.
I wish to make reference to one other thing the Minister of Trade and Commerce said the other afternoon which interested me a good deal. He referred to his hope that convertibility might come in the near future inside Europe. If I understood the minister correctly, he seemed to regard that with great satisfaction; and on the face of it, one would be inclined to regard it with satisfaction. On

The Budget-Mr. J. M. Macdonnell the other hand, I raise this question, Mr. Speaker. If we stand aside and allow Europe and presumably Britain-because the minister hoped that Britain would be included; and if Britain comes in, that means the sterling area, I take it-to make an arrangement, or if we stand by while all that part of the world reaches an arrangement as to convertibility, I wonder if that may not work greatly to our disadvantage. I am not prepared to dogmatize on that. I put it forward as a matter which I think is worthy of serious consideration. However that may be, my own feeling is that, so far as devaluation is concerned, so far as moving forward into freedom is concerned-and I have never suggested it should be done in any helter-skelter or ill-considered manner-it seems to me that we are not prepared to do it at all. We are standing pat. We are not moving forward. It is a kind of wait-and-see policy. I should like to remind the house of words which I read to it not so long ago, written by a highly respected publication, the London Economist, with regard to the British step taken last September, whereby they moved the pound down to a new fixed value. There was no loosening of the controls at all; they were just as tightly fastened as ever, except at a new figure. This is what the Economist says, and these words were written I think in the middle of October:
It is now clear that the opportunity of devaluation has been missed. Abroad there has been much disappointment, mixed with amazement that so sharp a reduction in the exchange value of the pound sterling was not accompanied by any relaxation whatsoever of the restrictions that keep the pound so tightly inconvertible. "Devaluation," says one experienced continental commentator, "is usually the price paid for getting rid of exchange control. To pay so high a price and get none of the rewards is a very bad business."
Meanwhile, Mr. Speaker, we are preparing for another trade conference at Torquay. You will remember that, following the one at Geneva, there was one last year at Annecy. Now we are to have one at Torquay. I raise the question whether we are going to have another frustration following on the two previous ones; because it seems to me that it will be in the highest degree unfortunate and lamentable if we do.
If I might digress for a moment, I should like to say that, when people survey what is going on now, when they realize the number of bilateral or two-sided trading arrangements which are being made-particularly, I am afraid, by the United Kingdom-and when they realize how important it is for us that we should have multilateral or many-sided trading agreements, it is not surprising that thoughtless people should be arguing for barter. Apparently there are some who think that barter is some strange, new, brilliant discovery of the twentieth century. They talk

about it really as though it were a substitute for the freedom which brought us where we are. They do not seem to realize that it is stepping back into a situation that we stepped out of generations ago. The other day I read an article apparently holding up to admiration a company-and indeed the company was entitled to admiration-which I think was in the lamp business, and which was selling lamps hither and yon throughout the world and taking goods in exchange: barter. One of the things I remember was that they got goat's hair in Turkey. That company undoubtedly deserves credit for its enterprise, but what I am commenting on is the state of affairs which thrust them into that kind of business. What it meant was that a man who was expert in the selling of lamps but who knew nothing about goat's hair had to try to learn about the business of selling goat's hair. It is just reverting to the situation which we should have got away from years and years ago.
What bothers me is that, from our good friend the minister down, I cannot find any sign of concern about the continuation of these controls. I often wonder if people forget that these were invented less than twenty years ago by the notorious Dr. Schacht as a totalitarian instrument. That is what they were. We took them over, at first with the hope that we would use them only for a short time and then get rid of them. I sometimes wonder whether people forget that it is freedom that has brought us as far as we have come, until just a few years ago. But to my great regret I find that instead of these controls being regarded as evil, unnatural and temporary, a good many people-and not only those who are using those implements-are coming to regard them as beneficent, natural and, if not permanent, at any rate quite indefinite. Those responsible I think admit that they probably will some day disappear, but there is no sense of urgency. Indeed, on the contrary, there is rather a sense of pride.
I do not think we need to be surprised at that. As to men who are using these powerful instruments-because consider the enormous power put in the hands of men by foreign exchange control-and, I think, using them skilfully, how can you expect that they will want to toss them away? Of course they think they are good. As I undertook to say a while ago, men who have been using them, particularly young men, would have to jump out of their intellectual skins to believe that these controls are not good. I would remonstrate with the minister however who comes out, not without some feeling of pride-indeed I think that was the only part of the budget which gave him much satisfaction-and tells us about the exchange reserve they were building up. I would remind him of two or

three things there. First of all, they only build up this reserve by controlling us this way and that, by shutting out this and by shutting out that and, as I said on another occasion, by turning off the tap and turning it on again.
Secondly, I would remind the minister that he has gone part of the way I have suggested to him repeatedly. Notwithstanding that the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) said that devaluation would bring chaos-that, of course, was during the election-notwithstanding that the Prime Minister assured us that devaluation would bring chaos, we have had devaluation. Of course I know the minister will say: "Oh, yes, we only did it because other people did it." But what I am suggesting to the minister is that we are strong enough to go on our own.
The other thing I want to point out to the minister-not that I want to take away whatever little pleasure he may get out of the budget-is this. I want to remind him that a great deal of the satisfaction which he has had in the building up of his reserves has come about by entirely fortuitous circumstances. Alberta oil has been the right bower. I hold in my hand an advertisement from today's Ottawa Citizen, which points out that western oil is saving 100 million scarce United States dollars this year. If that is an accurate statement, if it is actually saving 100 million scarce United States dollars which formerly we had to pay for oil, it is only the beginning of what it is doing for the exchange problem, because it is also bringing large investments of United States dollars, which are also helping the exchange situation.
I am not going to elaborate this further; but I do think that as we go on with this instrument which we have discovered, as we persist in this evil course, which is not a healthful one for the economy but unhealthful, we seem to be like a man who has found a cure for drunkenness. He says: "It is all right for me to drink now because I have the cure in my own hand, and I can keep the situation in hand."
I just want to summarize briefly what I have been saying about trade and about exchange control in connection with it. This division into economic blocs is going to do us endless harm. I should like again to refer to a quotation which I gave on a previous occasion from the international monetary fund report, pointing out that there are risks in accepting the more competitive conditions that come from freeing the exchanges and freeing controls. But they say:
Unless these risks are accepted, the improvement in the world economic situation made thus far may be replaced by deterioration.
The Budget-Mr. J. M. Macdonnell
That is the end of the quotation from the international monetary fund report of last year, but I should like to suggest that instead of the word "may" we had better put in the word "will", and that we can see the signs of it before us. In passing I should also like to mention what I think is often overlooked, namely, that as long as these fixed exchange rates remain they cut the nerve of international investment. I know we will be told that there has been much United States investment here. That is perfectly true. The lure of oil, and perhaps other lures have brought in large amounts, but nothing in the world like what could come if exchanges were free. Take a look at the condition of England and see what might happen to them if they were able to get freedom and with it international investment, the only thing that can enable them to bridge the dollar gap.
I want to remind the house of the meaning of the word "convertible". In plain words I would describe it as permitting you to spend anywhere money which you received for goods sold anywhere. In other words, that your money is convertible and can be used up and down the world. Incidentally, if we could reach that happy day, Mr. Speaker, the dollar problem by that time would have disappeared. There would be no dollar problem because money could circulate freely.
I am not suggesting that that could be done without some disturbances here and there; but I am suggesting that we in Canada by happy accident are in a position where we could do it with the minimum of disturbance. All the evidence is that our dollar, on whatever free market there is, has hovered within a fraction of a cent of the fixed rate for several months.
I would remind the minister again of the modesty of my request. I recognize that the treasury department might wish to begin by making the dollar convertible only on current account. They might think they had to begin in that partial way.
I would repeat that we in Canada are rather fond of holding ourselves out as examples in this or that department of life. I think it is good that we can, but I suggest that here would be the best place of all to hold ourselves out as an example, and to strike a blow for freedom. I say again that if the controls remain we may find in all likelihood that Torquay will be abortive, just as to a very large extent Geneva and Annecy were abortive.
One other point on this division into two economic blocs. It may be that the tremendous oil discoveries, tremendous iron ore discoveries and other discoveries burgeoning to an extent that we cannot see now, conceivably
