The Budget-Mr. J. M. Macdonnell may solve our own exchange problem; but I want to ask, what is going to happen to many primary producers in this country if we really are going to be cut off for any extended time from the sterling area.
I hope, Mr. Speaker, that the period of watchful waiting is near an end, and that we may be coming to a period of action.
I want to say a word about economy. The minister's warning underlined economy. But I have the feeling that the minister might have said a little more than he did, might have given us a little more lead in the matter. He said, as reported at page 1213 of Hansard:
The government became aware several months ago of these revenue prospects . . .
He had just been referring to the revenue.
The government became aware several months ago of these revenue prospects and of the desirability of keeping our expenditures this next year within the total revenue that we could foresee in the economic conditions I have described. We decided that we should plan to do this.
I am sure the minister did not think it was a very original idea to try to plan to cover expenditures, but at any rate he did have this idea. The minister says that they all got busy. The minister, the treasury board and the cabinet got busy. Then we have the minister's word for it that they made substantial reductions in the estimates before they came down. Of course we are left to imagine what they were before they came down; and one might ask the government whether it was only because of this emergency that they really grappled seriously with the problem of economy. It would be interesting to know what the new method was, how it worked, and how much they did cut down. But of course in the state in which we now find ourselves we would never expect to have information of that kind, because we find it exceedingly difficult to get even information to which we are fully entitled. Therefore the door will be banged, barred and bolted at that stage, and we shall have only what the minister tells us.
I think the ordinary citizen will feel that it is just not reasonable that you cannot economize a lot when you are spending $2,400 million. I think that is what he will feel, and he will not be very sympathetic when the minister says that only $310 million of it is civil service salaries. He will be inclined to say:	"Does the minister think
the other $2,100 million are sacred? Is nothing to be done about that?" Is the minister suffering from a kind of fatalism? Are these other $2,100 million like interest on debt or statutory commitments? Incidentally, many of them are, of course. They will agree I think with what the minister said further, namely, that "if we want services we must 

pay for them." That is a very fair observation, but it leads me to say this: Most of us in this house-in fact, nearly all of us-are unable to take the necessary steps to find out whether these services really are necessary. No hon. member in the house, apart from the minister and his close associates, has any true knowledge except through an interpreter. Of course all that the minister as an interpreter gives us is what might be called the end result. We hear nothing of what has gone on before. It reminds me of an incident that happened with an interpreter in a court in Toronto one day. There was a Chinese witness and a Chinese interpreter. The interpreter asked the witness quite a long question which perhaps took a minute to put. The witness answered also at considerable length,, let us say, almost a minute. At the end of the answer the interpreter turned to the court and said:	"He say 'no.' "
That was all the court got out of the long account, and I am sure that that is all we ever get from the minister. We get yes or no, the bare statement.
There are one or two items to which I should like to draw attention. For instance, we have the Department of Agriculture which apparently shows $7 million down. But, apart from the savings on western freight, which was down $12 million, we find that the estimates are really $5 million up.
There are decreases in the Department of Trade and Commerce; but on the other hand there is an increase of $1,170,000 in the national research council, which is the special child of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe). I do not know whether he calls it his, as he called the Polymer Corporation yesterday. In any event he has a great interest in it-and we may be very glad that he has.
All I have to say about these things is that they are good. But how good are they? How are we going to know how good they are, and whether we need to bear this great expense, unless we have some better method of informing the House of Commons, unless some better method is devised?
For instance, I saw the other day a beautiful little booklet describing one of the provinces. It was beautiful, and it must have been very expensive to produce. Someone has told me that there was a good deal of inaccuracy in it, but I have no comment to make on that. All I am saying is that that is done, and it must have cost a pretty penny. Yet there is no opportunity to discuss a thing of that kind, or to find out whether it was necessary or not. I submit the present system is really contrary to common sense. Indeed, I support the view expressed more than twenty

years ago by the former prime minister, the Right Hon. W. L. Mackenzie King, in which he said one or two things which I suggest are of some importance, and to which I hope hon. members will listen. He said this:
My hon. friend, the leader of the opposition, will recall that at the beginning of the session, I discussed with him the advisability of the different parties in the house adopting some more effective method of scrutinizing the supply requested by the government, some method which would enable members to hear what the officials of the departments had to say with respect to the several items included in the estimates.
And later he said:
Speaking for the government, I would say that we would welcome a change in the present method -a change which would not only afford fuller opportunity for discussion, but which would carry with it an obligation on the part of the heads of different branches of the public service to appear before a committee of the house and explain fully the reasons which have occasioned the recommendations which find their place in the estimates submitted to the house.
That is what was said by Mr. King in June of 1928.
Mr. Speaker, I point out to you and to hon. members that that is exactly the kind of thing we have been asking for; but, with the exception of the Department of External Affairs, we have no chance whatever of getting it.
If time permitted I would like to make further reference to the searching comment made by the auditor general, Mr. Sellar. However, I shall content myself with one further bit of evidence, this time from Great Britain, showing the extent to which they go in their effort to come to grips with these matters. This is evidence which was given before a select committee of the British house, and which is contained in. a report tabled in 1946. This describes the methods used by a certain committee to satisfy itself as to the propriety of certain expenditures. This is the information given by the clerk of committees:
It is true, of course, that they asked for any evidence that they thought would assist them in the inquiry that any sub-committee was engaged in.
If they were examining the expenditure, they not only went down to factories, but they had up as witnesses people who were actually engaged in this particular task in some form or other. I
I am not going to pursue this matter further than to say that, whatever is to be done, the present situation is unsatisfactory, and indeed contrary to common sense. No one in this house has ever seen a dollar struck off the estimates. All that happens is that we have a long talk which we hope our constituents will read, and then nothing is done.
When that statement was made twenty-two years ago by Mr. King our expenditures were about $366 million. They are now $2,400 55946-981
The Budget-Mr. J. M. Macdonnell million. I suggest that if our conduct was foolish then, it is seven times as foolish now, because we are spending seven times as much.
I should like to review the budget situation briefly, and then come to a conclusion. I have tried to show the house that the situation is clear, that the best we can do, even if things are good in the coming year, is to break even. The minister has assured us-and he may be lamentably right-that we need not expect expenditures below $2,400 million. Then, in the third place, he said that the government had buckled down to the task of keeping down the estimates-and he wants a good mark for that. Fourth, he said that in good years-and he does not refer to bad years-that in good years we must balance. My comment on that is that I think it is widely believed that expenditures are going to go up, and that it is widely feared that trade will come down.
I have pointed out that I think the minister's attitude is too negative, and summed up by saying that, failing conditions favourable beyond expectation, it is a case of either deficits or higher taxation.
In these circumstances one might have expected something like a clarion call from the government. However, I suggest to the minister that all we have had has been a quavering and uncertain sound-occasionally a dirge, then cheerfulness breaking in, but no clear lead.
True, there was reference to a shelf of public works to give support; but relief works are not a solution. There must be a relief works program for any emergency. What is needed is something more than that. The government must create a climate favourable to enterprise, and lead the way.
What are they doing? Well, if I may digress I shall refer to one special matter, which I think is of some importance, in which they are doing what I think is apt to have an adverse effect upon enterprise. Apparently the Department of National Revenue is now beginning to make use of the provision in the Income Tax Act whereby the officials of the department have the authority to force corporations to pay dividends which those corporations do not want to pay.
Let me say at once that I sympathize with with the department in its desire to prevent any tax evasion, and I am inclined to believe that they ought to have enough skill and astuteness in their ranks to do that.
But I also wish to say that for members of the department to step in and to overrule the decision of a company's executive as to what the proper reserve inside a company should be is verging-and I do not like to use a strong term-is verging on unwisdom

The Budget-Mr. J. M. Macdonnell of the most extreme kind. If there is any matter in connection with which the executive of a company ought to have the right to decide, I should think it would be on the extent of reserves.
May I underline that by placing on record some figures which astonished me. These are American figures, but I suggest the circumstances are sufficiently similar in this country to make them significant here. These figures disclose that it is estimated that this year in the United States ninety-two per cent of capital expenditures will come from depreciation and retained surplus. I do not say that it is all retained surplus; I say it is depreciation and retained surplus. That ninety-two per cent is coming from inside the revenues of the various corporations concerned. I point out that these surplus funds will be an absolute sheet anchor for investment, particularly if we run into times of slackened activity when we will wish to have expenditures made.
I cannot find words to express my feeling that interference of that kind is in the highest degree unwise. The natural inclination of companies is to pay dividends-except in respect of private companies which may be dealt with specially. The fact is that the ordinary company manager likes to pay a dividend. That is what the shareholders want, and his whole inclination will be to do it. To force him to use money which, in his discretion, he has set aside, and which will be available for the improvement of the company's plant and extension and all that sort of thing is, as I say, in the highest degree unwise.
I am not going to ask the minister to answer this question now as I will put it to him later on, but the rumour is that warnings have been given in many cases, and there are a few well authenticated cases, that there is a campaign on hand to try to clean out company surpluses. The men who are doing that are either very unwise or enemies of the system of private enterprise, because that should be one of the sheet anchors whereby private enterprise can prove its worth when the time comes to provide employment.
I am glad to be able to congratulate the minister on doing something-I hope it will turn out to be something substantial-to assist companies with small earnings. The minister promised last autumn that he would do that and I am glad to see that steps are being taken which I hope will prove to be effective.
I said a moment ago that we needed a clear call from the government, that we needed a climate favourable to enterprise,


that the government should take steps to help the people to help themselves. The government should get off the people's backs and give them a lead. In October, 1948, our party went on record as being in favour of the following policy:
In co-operation with the provinces to assist in the convention and development of our natural resources, and as one of the means to that end. to establish a national development advisory council.
Such a council would be made up of representatives of the provinces, of labour, of industry and of agriculture. At present we have merely an uncertain sound of helplessness and hopelessness and equally uncertain optimism instead of something of this kind. Such a council would have at its disposal the accumulated knowledge of its various members.
As an illustration of how the government can best co-operate with private initiative I would point out the mining industry. There you have the government giving a lead. The government makes surveys and provides information. The government suggests that such and such areas are likely to be fruitful and then the private individual comes along with his energy and initiative and steam and goes and does the job. Of course, the government should regulate and should tax, but the government should be the regulator and not the mainspring of the watch.
If we consider the possibilities in Canada today we look first of all at the western provinces where we have large resources. I was amazed to see a list of them the other day, things that I had never dreamed of. There we have resources of base metals which with the nearby coal and oil are capable of great expansion. The day has gone when we can regard the three prairie provinces as being merely agricultural. Alberta is already transformed and Saskatchewan may be well on the way. What is true of the prairie provinces can be true of the maritimes, and indeed true of every place.
It is unfortunately true that for strategic reasons we should strengthen ourselves in every way possible on the industrial side. This chimes in with the United States; partly because of their own defence program they will have a great need for the basic materials that we have. What a wonderful chance this offers for a true policy of "Canada first", a policy that could well redound to the benefit of other countries also so that we would have that best of all business arrangements where both sides are benefited.
On the other hand, if there is a failure to act we may find that we have missed the bus. The appearance of unemployment underlines the urgency of the need of action. Another

thing that is present in the minds of us all is the inescapable and overwhelming need of the democratic nations making it clear to all the world, particularly to that part which is in doubt and which is on balance as between democracy and communism, that we can provide a better way of life, not only in spiritual but in material things, than communism can ever do. It is obvious of course that if such a plan were carried out it would ease the tax burden by increasing the national income.
The minister concluded with what I thought was a rather odd note when he said:
If at some future time we have to face serious difficulties, we shall find that we have never been better equipped and prepared to resolve them.
That sounds all right, but I point out again that it is a defensive note. I doubt if any serious person will believe that our difficulties will occur at some future time. He would realize that they are here now. Therefore I say that the appropriate attitude of the government is not to end on this defensive note but to take the initiative, go out and meet these difficulties. I have suggested some ways in which I think it can all be done.
This party, even though in opposition, would support such an effort to the utmost of its capacity.
Mr. Speaker, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green):
That all the words after "that" to the end of the question be deleted and the following be substituted therefor:
"This house regrets that the policies of the government, as announced by the Minister of Finance,
(1)	make higher taxation inevitable:
(2)	make no adequate attempt to eliminate extravagance and avoid unnecessary expenditure; and
(3)	make no provision for a program of national development, without which there can be no hope of a reduction of taxation and the present high cost of living."

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my first word will be to pay tribute to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) for the presentation he made of the budget last Tuesday. In former years when he presented budgets to the house he made notable explanations of the measures he proposed, and last Tuesday's performance was no exception to the rule he established.
Before I go on to discuss the budget I should like to correct an error which appears at page 1389 of Hansard of March 30, 1950, the fourth line from the bottom, where the figure "$800 million" is reported. I understand that the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Thatcher) corrected this in Hansard before he left for home this week end but certain newspapers, particularly the Winnipeg Free Press and its subsidiaries, the
The Budget-Mr. Coldwell Regina Leader-Post and the Saskatoon Star-Phoenix, have been using this figure and saying there is some rift in the C.C.F. with regard to social security and unemployment. There is no rift.
Of course, the figure should be about $660 million as outlined in the government's statistics and statements. I hope that the newspapers which have erroneously taken this figure as being authentic will correct it accordingly. But a mistake of nearly $200 million is a substantial error.
There is one other matter about which I wish to say something before I proceed with a discussion of the budget. Yesterday, following the statement of the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) on the arrangements at The Hague last week, I asked him a question as to the extent to which similar steps to integrate economic arrangements had been taken under article 2 of the Atlantic treaty in order to eliminate conflict in international economic policies and to encourage immediately collaboration among members of the North Atlantic alliance. The minister's reply indicated that Canada had taken a keen interest in this article and had -and I know this is true-contributed a good deal to its acceptance in its present form. It is quite apparent, however, that nothing has been done yet in this regard.
We think that article 2 of the North Atlantic treaty is of vital importance in the maintenance of peace. As we have often said, while the world situation unfortunately demands close defensive arrangements among the western democracies, totalitarianism will not be stopped by military arrangements alone. It is essential that economic conditions shall be so arranged that rapid improvements in standards of living throughout the world shall be made. Surely we have learned the lesson that dictatorships are prone to arise among people who are oppressed and who suffer poverty, misery and want. The removal of the causes of poverty, misery and want must be a major consideration of the democratic nations. We believe that only in this way can the threat to democratic freedom be removed. We therefore urge Canada to press for the immediate implementation of article 2 of the North Atlantic treaty.
Turning to the budget, obviously the 1950 budget marks the end of an era in the eyes of the government. The post-war boom, kept going by the necessity of aiding in European reconstruction as well as by the endeavour of private business to re-tool and convert from war to peace, is apparently drawing to a close. I think this is a fair interpretation to put upon the considerations advanced by the
1528	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Coldwell Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) in his budget speech. The tremendous wartime and postwar capital investment programs undertaken by industry have largely been responsible for the soaring prices and much of the inflation we have experienced since the war. Public and private expenditures have risen year by year to a phenomenal level with the result that until recently there was not only full employment but actually a shortage of manpower as well as many vital materials.
The high level of business activity and the huge capital expenditure program have resulted also in unprecedented business profits. I do not propose to deal with that aspect of our economy as I have done usually in discussing budgets on former occasions. Obviously the recession in labour demand this past winter and the diminution in the volume of our overseas trade have caused the government to introduce this year a budget that is very different indeed from the one introduced last year. I say it appears therefore that we are witnessing the end of the post-war inflationary period, and consequently now is the appropriate time to do some stock-taking. That is what I propose to do this afternoon rather , than to go into a detailed analysis of the budget.
My main criticism of the new budget is that the government seems prepared to accept whatever levels of production, employment and economic activity the uncontrolled, undirected and unplanned operations of the private enterprise system may bring to us. This was apparent when the minister gave us his forecast of revenue and expenditure for 1950-51. He stated that it was his expectation:
. . . that in general our national employment and income will be sustained at approximately the present level ...
He then went on to express the opinion that:
Should conditions be better than this-as they could be if everything goes well-my forecast will be more than realized. Should economic conditions deteriorate, as they could, our revenue will fall off and our expenditure increase, as compared with the figures I am now putting forward.
In other words, Mr. Speaker, the government seems content to float along with the tide and the winds of fine or foul weather, the ebb and flow of economic activity, if you like. There is no suggestion that the ship of state will be set on a more favourable tack or that the auxiliary engines will be used if she runs into adverse winds or a strong ebb tide. The government has set no other course than that of taking the gamble that the winds will be favourable, the economic tide with us, and the weather clear. Therefore the minister


budgets for a surplus. The economic uncertainty about which he warned us was underlined when he said:
I should like to emphasize that our tax structure now is such that it is very sensitive to changes in employment and incomes, and relatively modest changes in these can have a more than proportionate effect upon our revenue.
I take it that every hon. member will agree with this statement, but in our view changes in employment and income need not, and indeed should not, remain beyond our control. It is at this point that we of the C.C.F. part company with the government, and indeed with all those who believe that we must leave our economic welfare to the chance decisions of individuals and corporations who occupy key positions in the economy of the nation.
The minister made it quite clear that in his opinion the central government should play an extremely limited role in promoting full employment and maximum production. He described the role of the government as fourfold. The first point he made was the creation of a favourable climate for enterprise, whatever that may mean. I noticed that the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell), who resumed his seat a few moments ago, also took the point of view that the extent of the duty of the government was to create a favourable climate. The second point the minister made was in regard to the planning of the timing and placing of public works expenditures. Apparently, from recent statements made by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), this should be done only when the municipalities and the provinces cannot cope with the pressing problem of unemployment. Only then should the federal government be asked to assist. I might remark that this is a return to the same kind of psychology that we knew in the 1930's when the central government took the view that the initiative must first come from the municipalities and then from the provinces. The third point was that the government should accept some special responsibility for the promotion and development of our basic primary industries. Well, I think the budget makes provision for certain primary industries, in a sense. What the minister means, I take it, is that such tax concessions as those given to the mining and oil industries should be continued and indeed expanded; and again I find that the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell) is in full accord with that point of view.
The fourth point is that the budget makes some vague reference to readiness to co-operate with other governments, municipal and provincial, in meeting regional problems that threaten nation-wide economic repercussions.

I draw attention particularly to the qualification "regional problems". There is no indication on the part of the government that it is prepared to accept responsibility for either the maintenance of full employment or agricultural prosperity, and in our view that kind of responsibility must be accepted by democratic governments. I want to say as emphatically as I can that in this way only can the challenge of totalitarianism be met by free peoples. What I think the government fails to recognize, and what many hon. members of this house may not have recognized yet, is that the world is moving toward new forms of economic and social associations. That is, we are making a transition from the old to the new, and we of the C.C.F. believe that in doing this we must take every step we can to conserve that which is good in our present social relationship, while we consciously plan to assist in the evolution of the new. The precious rights of free association, free expression, freedom of worship and so on must be maintained; for these, I think in the view of all hon. members of this house, are among the fundamentals of a free society.
But let me add immediately that even in our own country these freedoms cannot be freely exercised by all. 'The man who fears loss of employment, the man who holds minority views, sometimes religious, sometimes political, is not always free to express his views. Nor are the thousands of farmers and workers who fear loss of markets for their produce or who fear unemployment, nor the businessmen who fear a business recession, completely free. For them and because of them-and they represent the vast majority of our constituents from one end of this country to the other-the planning of our economic resources and activities should be the first consideration of a democratic government.
Now I want to say very clearly and distinctly that in our view such planning does not require the establishment of an all-powerful state, nor does it require regimentation. Indeed, in our present society we have a great deal of planning by nation-wide corporations, which sometimes are monopolies in their own fields. They plan in their own, and often conflicting, interests which from time to time prove injurious to the nation as a whole. So I say it is not a question of planning or not planning our economic activities; rather the question is in whose interests we shall plan, and by what agencies it shall be undertaken. There is no indication in the budget speech or in statements by the government that any conscious attempt is contemplated to maintain maximum production and full employment;
The Budget-Mr. Coldwell and I suggest that there is no other institution or agency in our democratic society qualified to undertake those tasks but this parliament or bodies set up under its authority and responsible to it. Last spring the government and its supporters across the country promised to maintain both full employment and maximum production and prosperity. That promise was made in 1945 as well. I ask them to say now, flatly and in plain English, whether or not they are prepared to fulfil the pre-election pledges made to the Canadian people in this respect. If so, in formulating the budget proposals the government should have placed before this house its plans for the maintenance, and indeed the expansion, of production and employment. Instead of this, what did the minister say? He hoped and expected that employment and income would be sustained at present levels, but warned that economic conditions might deteriorate. There was no suggestion that the government itself had a responsibility to maintain the one or prevent the other; nor indeed, as far as this house knows, has it any plans to do so, except the willingness already mentioned to co-operate with municipal or provincial governments in meeting regional problems, and again only if they threaten nation-wide economic repercussions. I would remind hon. members that the government refused this winter to present plans to give employment to the four hundred thousand who were seeking work at the time.
We hear talk of accumulating surpluses in some manufacturing industries, as well as in agriculture; as the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) put it, a little bit of cheese, a little bit of butter, and some honey. That was the way he put it before the actual figures were revealed; and those figures were rather disturbing. In some industries such as clothing and footwear, the manufacture of washing machines and in hardware sales, there is a falling off in the volume of business. Not long ago I read the speeches of the presidents of two of our largest farm implement companies, Massey-Harris and Cockshutt. Both stated that their sales in 1950 might be less than in 1949. That was the warning they gave their shareholders.
The trouble is that private enterprise or capitalism, if you prefer to call it so, is an economy which functions fairly well only when goods are being used up rapidly, as in war or in reconstruction, and generally in times of scarcity. As soon as capital construction and the tooling of factories are complete, and goods appear in abundance, purchasing power slackens and production slows down, sometimes ceasing altogether. Consequently in the last hundred years or so

The Budget-Mr. Coldwell we have seen periods of prosperity during wartime, followed by shorter or longer periods of activity and prosperity in the postwar interval, and then almost inevitably a slump. Abundance presents private enterprise capitalism with an insoluble problem which no financial juggling can hide or cure.
We are convinced that this need not be, that we are endowed with sufficient intelligence to be able to plan to meet these ups and downs, these booms and depressions, and to give measures of security such as the world has not known, at least in recent times. So we say plans should be made to guarantee the maintenance of full production as long as people anywhere in the world lack food, clothing, and homes. I say that, until these elementary requirements both in our land and elsewhere have been met, there should be no talk of curtailing production, no talk indeed of impending recession or depression. On the contrary, there should be a continuous expansion. The proper use of our manpower, our machines, and our resources should be organized and planned to provide a standard of living and security for all our people such as we can only dream about today.
I noticed that the hon. member for Greenwood brought a new note to the fore in his address this afternoon when he referred to the resolution of the Progressive Conservative party in the fall of 1948 when some idea of planning was involved in the resolution to which he drew the attention of the house. I say that by planning the proper use of our manpower, our machines and our resources we could provide a high standard of living for all our people, and create surpluses with which we could help raise living standards throughout the world, such as we can only dream of today.
I remember that prior to the war, during the depression, I made a statement in which I said that if our resources, our machines and our manpower were fully employed, we could produce the equivalent of $4,000 per year for every family of five in Canada. At the time this statement was ridiculed, though I neither said nor implied-indeed, I said the opposite -that all this production would be available for consumption goods, or that it could be divided thus equally, or that it could not be. But in the excellent speech he made on his estimates last Friday the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe), stated that our national production in 1948 was equal to an average of $1,200 per capita or, putting it as I did before the war, in terms of a family of five, exactly $6,000 per family.
With proper planning of production and of trade we believe that figure could be further

increased and the standard of living of most people vastly improved. In our opinion this will not be achieved by trusting to automatic adjustments in an unplanned economy. Experience has shown that there is no automatic tendency in the present economic system, capitalism, for spending to keep up to output. Sometimes spending runs ahead of output and we get high prices and inflation. At other times spending lags far behind output and we get depression, business bankruptcy and unemployment. In our opinion this is accounted for, first, because profit margins diminish as capital becomes plentiful and hence private industry lacks incentive to expand; and second, because the unequal distribution of wealth gives some people less than they need to spend and others more than they can manage to spend. Years ago it was a good thing for society for people to have much more than they could manage to spend; for when machines were few and production was slow, there was a problem of saving sufficient for capital expansion, from which industry could borrow from the savings of thousands of people. Today I heard the hon. member for Greenwood complain about the income tax department attacking the undistributed profits of corporations. As a matter of fact, today one of the difficulties in the present phase of capitalistic society is that the savings of the ordinary people cannot find suitable places for investment largely because large corporations are accumulating reserves out of which they can make their own expansion without public borrowing. Consequently our banking and lending system is becoming far less important to industry than it was in days gone by.
I should add that now the principle, widely accepted by many economists, is that the level of spending needs to be planned and maintained if slumps are to be avoided. I think that was the lesson which we were taught in the 1930's. But in spite of some storm signals which may or may not foreshadow a storm during this current year, the government's budget includes no plan to meet any threat to our economy. The erratic fluctuations of private capital are a prime cause of boom and of depression. It is, in our opinion, the task of government so to plan the economy that the amount of spending by government, by business, and by consumers is in the aggregate sufficient to buy all we can produce or obtain in exchange for the things we produce, including of course provision for capital goods and expansion. This, surely, is the central problem of economic stability to which democratic governments must give attention if we are to withstand and to defeat the threats of totalitarian communism or equally the threat of

some form of totalitarian fascism. Not only this, but we have always to remember that our social welfare program depends upon the maintenance of a sound economic foundation. Such a program of social security must be enlarged substantially if the Canadian people are to be assured of that national health and social security system which modern democracies expect as of right. This I say is another reason why we should give attention to the intelligent planning of our economic activities.
The government should therefore, in its budgetary proposals, present a plan for the maximum employment of our manpower, our industries, our resources, and for the maximum production of goods. This the budget does not do. A great British Liberal economist-and I draw the attention of the house to the fact that he is a Liberal economist-Sir William Beveridge, now Lord Beveridge, put this well a few years ago when he wrote:
Adoption of a national policy of full employment means a revolution in national finance-a new type of budget . . . What is the essence of this new budgetary policy? It is that the budget is made with reference to available manpower, not to money; that it becomes, in Mr. Bevin's phrase, a "human budget". Manpower is a datum; it cannot be altered by state action; to take anything else as a datum and to try to fit use bf manpower to it is to risk mass unemployment or mass fatigue. It follows that the minister of national finance has to take each year one cardinal decision; after estimating how much, assuming full employment and under the taxation which he proposes, private citizens may be expected to lay out that year on consumption and private investment, he must propose for that year public outlay sufficient, with this estimated private outlay, to employ the whole manpower* of the country, that is to say sufficient to make the assumption of full employment come true. This cardinal decision involves a break with the two main principles which have governed the state budgets of the past; first, that state expenditure should be kept down to the minimum necessary to meet inescapable needs; second, that state income and expenditure should balance each year.
Then he went on to suggest some means by which total spending or outlay should be controlled; and if I may be permitted to summarize what he implies, and what I think is pretty sound, it is this: First, consumers' expenditure can be raised or lowered by changes in taxation and by the social security policies of the government. Second, private capital expenditure can be influenced by credit policy and by the rate of interest influenced by our central banking policy. As I have already indicated, private capital expenditure is the most unstable element in our economy. That is why the C.C.F. advocates that some of our great key industries should be publicly-owned to give the government a greater measure of direct control over the capital expenditures in this vital sector of the economy. Then, of course,
The Budget-Mr. Coldwell capital expenditure by the government and by various government agencies, for example, crown and other public corporations, can be directly regulated and changes in capital expenditure in this sector can be used to some extent to offset fluctuations in the private sector. Therefore in a mixed economy the public sector can be used to protect the economy against the fluctuations in the private sector. The greater the degree of public ownership the easier it will be to take effective action to prevent a major slump.
The planning I have outlined would, of course, require the organization of a national planning commission or national investment board responsible through the government to parliament. I want to say here that it does not involve setting up a sort of super cabinet; and that such a body should be representative of a number of interests in the community, namely, government, labour, agriculture, industry, co-operative societies and so on, and in each of these the consumers' interests would be represented. The proposals of the national planning board or commission established under the authority of parliament would be brought here in broad outline for approval. That would be the function of parliament. This is not a new principle, and indeed it is not necessarily a socialist idea. For anyone who will read that profound study of finance and economy by the late Lord Keynes, "The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money", will find that he suggests that, in the next phase of social progress, that kind of thing will have to be undertaken.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I do not think that his sway is as absolute as it used to be.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
No; I quite agree that Lord Keynes' sway may not be as absolute as it used to be; world thinking has passed beyond the point at which it was when Lord Keynes wrote this particular study of employment, interest and money and the other books that he wrote outlining his theory. I think we have passed beyond that. I said that there would also have to be development programs and other projects to meet the specific problems of regional unemployment. Let us not forget that the Canadian economy is particularly vulnerable to seasonal unemployment, and specific measures will have to be planned to stimulate employment in our slack periods when there is seasonal unemployment.
Our vital export trade must be protected through long-term contracts and other beneficial controls so that we do not suffer more than is absolutely necessary from slumps in other countries which endeavour to export their domestic unemployment, in the form of goods which they are prepared to dump upon

The Budget-Mr. Coldwell the world market. Our external markets must be made as secure as possible and we must not shrink from the controls necessary to achieve that objective. We do not believe in controls for the sake of exercising control; but we do believe that certain beneficial controls in the interest of most of the people should be put into effect by the government when such controls are necessary to protect the great masses of the people of our country. We have seen what the recent lifting of controls has done in the field of rent. Many people have been unable to compete with those who have longer purses for the accommodation that they need. Our external markets must be made as secure as possible, as I have said before, and we must not shrink from anything that is necessary today to protect those markets. I say that Lord Keynes' ideas may be somewhat out of date now, but nevertheless a study of what he has to say in this connection would be quite interesting.
Furthermore, we are convinced, as I have indicated, that the government must socialize some of our major industries in order to permit the degree of planning necessary to achieve and maintain full employment and maximum production. There will always be severe limitations on our democracies as long as great economic power remains in the hands of small private minorities. So, Mr. Speaker, this afternoon what I have tried to do is to advocate a new approach to our national budgeting. I believe that with a full and proper use of our resources and manpower we can provide a rising standard of living and a comprehensive social security system from the cradle to the grave for all our Canadian people. In a growing community such as Canada is, where so many things need doing, there should always be more jobs available than there are workers to fill them.
I should like to add one last word, for my time is almost up. As I said at the outset,
I believe the world is witnessing a transition from the economy of private production for private gain to one of public enterprise for the common good. The problem of modern statesmanship in all the western nations, so it appears to us, is how best, how speedily, and with the least dislocation in bringing this about, the maximum distribution of volumes of commodities can be secured.
Time may not be on the side of the slow-moving democracies. Millions are demanding the right to a sufficiency of food, clothing and shelter. If dictatorships, while denying, to those who have never enjoyed them, those precious freedoms of thought, speech, association and worship we take for granted-if,

I say, dictatorships can provide that social and economic welfare which we could provide so much better but do not, then we shall lose the battle for real democracy and freedom.
And so, Mr. Speaker, in order to place our views more clearly on the record I wish to move, seconded by the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis):
That the amendment be amended by deleting therefrom all the words after the words "Minister of Finance" and by inserting instead thereof the following words:
(1)	indicate that the government is prepared to accept the present level of production as adequate for this country and as placing a limit on the services and security to be provided for our people; and
(2)	make no provision for increased national production through economic planning, public control of investment, public ownership of monopolistic industries, and the full and proper development and use of our resources, so as to ensure a rising standard of living and comprehensive social security for the Canadian people.
Before resuming my seat 1 should like to read the amendment as it will appear when amended, thus making it more intelligible. It would then read:
This house regrets that the policies of the government, as announced by the Minister of Finance,
(1)	indicate that the government is prepared to accept the present level of production as adequate for this country and as placing a limit on the services and security to be provided for our people; and
(2)	make no provision for increased national production through economic planning, public control of investment, public ownership of monopolistic industries, and the full and proper development and use of our resources, so as to ensure a rising standard of living and comprehensive social security for the Canadian people.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my first words must be words of congratulation to the minister on the presentation of his budget. I suppose the stylish and popular thing for me to do would be to think up a good many nasty things to say about it. However, I do not think that I shall waste my energies in an effort to do any such thing. I would prefer to think of it in another way, and use my energies to put before the house some constructive criticism.
I know many Canadians are very much disappointed because the minister did not provide further relief from taxation this year. In particular they feel the sales tax should have been abolished. In the light of what I shall have to say later, I think there is no good reason why their desire should not have been granted this year. Goodness knows, they have been asking for it long enough, and for the major reason that the sales tax does contribute so much to the high cost of living.

The government, of course, appear to think that they have the right to tell the people of Canada what they are going to get. That brings me to a phase of the budget, in the statement the minister made the other day, which I think will be of interest to all Canadians, and that is the question as to what should be the functions of a national government.
The last issue of The Montrealer says this:
There are some badly distorted ideas around today about just what the functions of a national government should be. Basically, the government is an organization set up by the people to run the affairs of the country for the benefit of the people. However, when the government attempts to become the master of the people by making the people dependent upon it, then the people and their very country are in grave danger.
I think we can all pretty well agree on that -at least I agree with it. However, in his budget speech, after a brief discussion of the unemployment in the past winter, the minister reminded the house that a central government cannot and, indeed, should not attempt to assume responsibility for all these regional problems. Then he attempted to define what he thought the role of a central government should be. His views are set out at page 5(a) of the mimeographed document he placed in the hand's of the leaders of the different parties immediately prior to presenting his budget. He did outline the four factors which make up what he said was the role of the central government.
I am not going to read those into the record, because they have already been dealt with by previous speakers. I noticed, however, that he omitted what I thought were two of the most important functions of government. These are, first, to conduct government in accordance with the will of the people and in their interests-not in the interests of those who sit on the front benches of a political party-not at all. The second thing which I consider a very important role of central government is the removal of all those barriers and artificial restrictions which deprive individual Canadians of the opportunity to achieve for themselves and their families economic security and freedom. If those two things were included in the minister's concept of the role of central government, I feel that I could go a long way with him. No central government with authority over financial policies can possibly divest itself of these responsibilities which I have mentioned, and still be called democratic. So the people, I am sure, will call the minister and his colleagues to account for neglecting to include these two all-important things in their concept of the role of a central government.
I have another compliment for the minister. I like him, as I have said many times before.
The Budget-Mr. Low
I think he is a young man of great ability. One of these days he is going to have a new approach to financial policy; and when he does I am satisfied that he will have the courage to do his budgeting along those lines.
The compliment I wish to pay to the minister at this stage is this: I do not believe any government in modern times, at least within my knowledge, here in Ottawa, has succeeded in estimating so closely expenditures and revenues. That is an achievement, in a day like this when our budget runs between $2,400 million and $2,500 million. That is a real achievement. I wish to congratulate the minister upon having scrutinized the financial affairs of this country, and having appraised them so closely.
I believe at this stage I should say one thing, perhaps not by way of criticism, but by way of suggestion. It has already been mentioned by the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell). I do believe that members of the House of Commons could be of greater help to the government, and certainly could discharge their responsibilities to the people of Canada better, if the estimates of expenditures were to be sent to committees set up for the purpose of giving them careful scrutiny and study.
I have had some experience in the committee on external affairs, in the last five years. During each of those years we have studied in a detailed manner the estimates for that department. After meetings of that committee I have felt as if we had come to grips with the details and with the facts. We were able to call before us experts from the department and we asked them all the questions we could think of. We got from them the reasons why this or that expenditure was necessary. In other words, we assured ourselves that there was a real need for everything that was proposed. When we came back into the house we felt as if we had done something like our duty. That is impossible under our present system of studying estimates in the house. It is utterly impossible with a committee as large as we have to apply ourselves diligently to that matter. As you well know, the tendency in this chamber is to give speeches and not to get down too much to fine details of consideration.
I urge the government to consider dividing the house into committees for at least a preliminary study of the estimates so that we may feel as though we are discharging our responsibilities to the people of Canada, and so that we can go back to them and say that we have given these things careful study and have assured ourselves that the government is following a policy of real economy; so that we can say that we know that because

The Budget-Mr. Low
we have gone into the details. That is the assurance I would like to be able to give my people. There are a great many advantages in this but I have not time to deal with them today.
In his budget address the minister forecast a national product of some sixteen and a quarter billion dollars in 1950-51. In 1948-49 we produced $16,000 million worth of goods and services. Those are staggering figures and they seem all the more remarkable when we remember that the total production for 1937-38 was $3,500 million. When we contemplate the huge increase in our actual yearly production during the past ten years we must all feel proud of our country. To produce in a year enough material wealth so that each family, as the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) said, may enjoy in the aggregate $6,000 worth or, to reduce it to consumer goods available, more than $4,600 worth a year, is a real achievement. That is exactly what we did in 1948-49.
What is more, we have not reached anything like the peak of our productive ability. It is not inconceivable, at least to me, that if our farms and our factories and other enterprises were operated to their optimum capacity we could produce $20,000 million worth of available goods and services in this country, and that with very little change in the organization of our enterprises.
But the question I am led to ask when I contemplate that staggering volume is this: Can we distribute it? That is a matter for serious consideration. That is the biggest question we face today. Judging from the experience of the past I doubt greatly whether Canada's distribution mechanism could possibly place these wanted goods and services in the hands of the consumers so that they could be used and enjoyed. When I say "enjoyed" I am taking a different stand on this whole problem of economics from the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar. We in this group do not lay stress on full employment, we say there should be full enjoyment. Surely our Canadian people are more entitled to a fair distribution of the leisure time made possible by mechanization and the introduction of laboursaving devices than they are to being kept with their noses to the grindstone for a specific period, I do not care what it may be.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: We do not disagree with that.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar interpolates that he does not disagree with that. I am glad he does not. Hon. members of the house would do well to give serious consideration to something the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch) placed on the record the other day, to be found at pages 1380 and 1381 of Hansard of March 30, 1950.

The facts and figures there set out should be studied by earnest people everywhere, and I especially commend them to those who have had some experience in accounting.
There is a widespread habit among Canadians of looking upon the terms "gross national production" and "national income" as being one and the same thing. I have heard cabinet ministers and other hon. members speaking as though they believed the market value of the national product and the national income were synonymous. That is not so. The national income invariably is less than the market value of our total production. That is true of Canada and I think it may be said to be true of all highly industrialized nations. Because the national income in any period is always less than the gross national product, surpluses accumulate.
If those surpluses are allowed to grow you will have either the destruction of valuable goods or the reduction of production. I think the reduction of production in a day like this would be a crime against society. If production is curtailed an increase in unemployment is inevitable, you reduce the standard of living for the masses of the people, and there is a serious shrinkage in income tax base.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) must realize that if the base for income tax assessment becomes much smaller he will simply not be able out of taxation to maintain a level of expenditure of $2,400 million which he said we must somehow continue to cope with even in the absence of large scale economic difficulties or widespread unemployment. I think the minister must have had a few bad moments when he contemplated that statement that he wrote into his budget and from which I have just quoted his own words. Not many sentences further on he said:
In years when economic conditions are adverse we must expect not only lower revenues but higher expenditures to assist in overcoming those economic difficulties and to maintain satisfactory levels of employment and income.
Those words would indicate to me a sober burst of realism, but what the minister failed to tell us was how he would finance higher expenditures out of a seriously shrunken tax base. For instance, how will he extract $530 million of income tax from individual Canadians if the total money income of the people is allowed to shrink during what the minister may call adverse years? That calls for serious contemplation and I think when the minister presents his rebuttal he ought to make clear to us how he would in times of adverse economic conditions get the money with which to keep expenditures up to a level of $2,400 million a year, which it would appear we have pretty well committed ourselves to spend.

I do not believe the minister has access to authentic information about all those factors in our economy which might bring on adverse economic conditions. We have never had competent technicians investigate and report on the potential productive capacity of Canada and the factors which make our national money income insufficient to move the gross national product of Canada. In this respect we have lagged away behind our neighbour the United States. We cannot afford to face the future without all the authentic facts we can possibly get from the fullest possible scientific investigation. The people of Canada certainly are entitled to have those facts.
The minister and his colleagues should think back to 1934 when President Hoover's administration appointed sixty engineers, technicians and economists to make a survey of the potential productive capacity of the United States as well as of those factors which obviously were making the national money income unable to move the gross national product. This body of experts under the chairmanship of Dr. Harold Loeb made a thorough analysis of the relationship between the national income and the national product. They issued their report in 1935 and it was published under the title, "The Chart of Plenty." You may not like to listen to what I say, and of course I would not blame you at all for that, but this report made by sixty technicians, engineers and economists of the United States is something that no one in this country can afford to ignore at a time like this. I want to quote three short excerpts from the conclusions that this investigating committee reached after a most intensive study of the situation in the United States. Turning first to page 71 I find this conclusion:
The budget line shown in heavy dots on the chart by its (general) location to the left of the capacity line clearly shows the destitution of the American people was due in 1929 to poverty and not to scarcity. The majority of the commodities listed could have been produced in desired amounts but could not have been sold at asked or profitable prices. The total national monetary income in 1929 did not equal the total price asked for the goods which could have been produced by the plant then existing. But instead of dropping prices until monetary income was able to command full production (which is the classical answer to this situation), prices were maintained and production was restricted. Consequently, national monetary income did not in 1929, nor does it today, command the full production of our industrial plant. Which is another way of saying that the national income was not what it should have been. In fact, since 1929 the national monetary income has been commanding an ever-decreasing volume of consumer goods and the actual national income has become but a fraction of the possible national income.
That calls for serious consideration. I should also like to refer to a short statement made by this committee on page 159 of their report. The statement that I am about to
The Budget-Mr. Low
read from the report was made after the committee had set up a chart showing that the average dollar value of goods produced per worker in the United States increased from $1,648 in 1869 to $6,533 in 1932, and that during the same sixty-odd year period average wages income per worker rose from $302 to only $1,096. After contemplating that and making a careful study of the reason why, they had this to say in their report:
Thus it is clearly evident . . . that the increasing productivity per worker in the past sixty years has not been translated into a proportionate increase in the standard of living of the population. It would seem that under the open market system this increased productivity per worker is prevented from effecting the improved living level one would expect by the related alternative measures of: (a) preparing for and waging war; (b) excessive reconstruction and expansion of plant, an orgy of saving made possible by the practice of creating money for purposes of private profit by means of the bank-credit mechanism.
Again on page 161 there is this very terse conclusion:
Since the present economic system has no means of distributing goods and services in excess of an amount which provides little more than subsistence for those possessing no property income, either the present system of rewarding labour must be discarded, or the plant and personnel must be operated at two-thirds' speed, or one-third unneeded productivity must be diverted into waging war, preparing for war, or some new large-scale speculative undertaking whose nature has not yet been envisaged.
This is the dilemma of society as exposed by the study of the national survey of potential product capacity. It would seem that the simple and obvious way out, that of giving a buying power adequate to procure desired goods and services to the limit of our ability to produce them, might well be tried.
I emphasize that.
Mr. Cold well: May I ask what the title of the book is?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
This book is "The Chart of Plenty" which was issued by the committee set up by the Hoover administration to investigate the whole of the United States economy and report on it. I want to repeat that last portion:
This is the dilemma of society as exposed by the study of the national survey of potential product capacity. It would seem that the simple and obvious way out, that of giving a buying power adequate to procure desired goods and services to the limit cf our ability to produce them, might well be tried.
As I say, Mr. Speaker, hon. members probably would not like simply to listen to me, but they cannot afford to laugh off the serious conclusions of men of the calibre of those who were on that committee, conclusions which were made after very careful study of the whole situation in the United States. The main conclusions of the committee of experts appointed by the Hoover administration have been confirmed in more

The Budget-Mr. Low
recent times than 1935 toy a good many first-ranking economists. I only have time to refer briefly to one of them now. As I said before, you may not feel inclined to listen to me, but I say with humility that I 'have prepared nearly three times the number of budgets that the minister has, I have presented them in parliament, and I have defended them, so that I have learned a few realities about sources of supply, tax bases, and attempting to balance a budget within the limits of our present system. We had better take cognizance of what thinking men are saying.
I want to refer now to one particularly whom we cannot afford to disregard. I refer to none other than Professor C. E. Ayres who for eighteen years has headed the department of economics at Texas university. A man who has held the chair of economics in a large university for over eighteen years must have something on the ball. Professor Ayres undertook an independent study along the same lines as that pursued in 1934 and 1935 by the committee to which I have referred, which was appointed by President Hoover. In 1946 Professor Ayres issued his report under the title of "The Divine Right of Capital". At page 33 of the book he has this to say, by way of conclusion to the portion of the work covered up to that point:
What we have learned as a result now seems obvious indeed.
He means as a result of his studies since 1929.
The economic heretics have been trying all along to make us see it. No economy could swing back and forth so wildly from one extreme to the other without there being something very wrong about it. There is indeed something very wrong with ours. It, fails to distribute mass-consumer purchasing power in sufficient quantity to permit the entire product of industry to be purchased. This failure exists at all times under capitalism and is noxious at all times.
There is nothing at all equivocal about that. Then he sums up his solution, or at least an answer to it, on page 95 in these terse words:
What we require, and all we require, to make the industrial economy work is a flow of mass-consumer purchasing power sufficient to absorb the entire product of industry at whatever level of production we may be able to achieve. This would not bring Utopia. It would not solve all problems. On the contrary, it would solve only one problem, the crisis into which we have been thrust by the institutions and dogmas of absolute capitalism. But this problem is the most important one we face today in this sense. If we solve this problem, then we shall have an opportunity to tackle others. If we do not, all our present problems will merge in the general collapse of the present structure of western society.
It seems to me those are words of gravity, which should serve as a warning to the people today. There you have the problem,

Mr. Speaker, and in a general way the answer. But I notice a complacent attitude on the part of many hon. members who seem to think that social services, especially the payment of family allowances, will close the gap between the national income and the gross national product. This is not so, as long as family allowances depend upon taxation. They are paid with money taken out of an already inadequate national income, through taxation. Family allowances are desirable, and in a measure they do help to keep up consumer demand for our production. But it must be clear to anyone who thinks about it that paying family allowances by taxing the money from the people is merely redistributing part of the national income that we have shown is already far too small to distribute our total production. And what aggravates the situation is that our present system of taxation makes it possible for practically the whole taxation burden to be shifted to the ordinary consumer with the lower income. He pays the shot principally through tax-inflated prices of the things he has to purchase in order to live. Therefore family allowances, under the present technique of getting the money to pay them, do not_ and cannot possibly close the gap between national income and national production. Surpluses of vitally needed goods will continue to pile up to embarrass our economy, throw men out of work, and bring us face to face with depression and suffering, unless we can do something fundamentally sound to take care of those surpluses.
Already the United States is facing serious economic problems. Already in that country vast surpluses of food and other materials have accumulated that cannot be moved into the hands of consumers; yet large sections of the population are not getting enough to eat. The last two issues of Life magazine, which I am sure most hon. members have seen, have brought home to us all the fact that huge surpluses do exist there and that unemployment and privation in some areas are present in serious proportions. Therefore poverty in the midst of plenty is again rearing its head. What is happening in the United States could happen here, because our economic and financial techniques are similar, and conditions in that country do have a strong influence on our own country.
It is gratifying, however, to see that some prominent thinkers in the country to the south are applying themselves to this great problem of making the national income equal to its task of distributing equitably the gross national production. The articles in Life magazine are a good indication of this concern. I was interested also in a United Press article which appeared in the Montreal Star

under the dateline Washington, March 31. I should like to quote it, because it is a good example of the kind of constructive thinking that is going on among at least some prominent officials. It is headed "Feed U.S., Senator urges", and reads:
Senator George D. Aiken, R., Vermont, said today that government subsidies should be used to provide extra food for the more than ten million Americans who don't get enough to eat.
Think of that; ten million of them.
He said his plan of government "food allotments" for low income families would solve the "twin-problem" of malnutrition and mounting food surpluses.
Aiken, ranking G.O.P. member of the senate agriculture committee, said his plan wouldn't cost much more, if any, than is being spent now to keep food off the market.
He also opposed the government's controversial Brannan plan for direct subsidy payments as unworkable and too costly.
In a speech prepared for a thirteen-state dairy conference, Aiken estimated that farm supports now cost about $1 billion a year.
"With mounting surpluses and increasing unemployment there is no time to be lost in meeting the challenge head on," he said.
This would indicate that there are people who are beginning to take more cognizance of the situation. On many occasions my colleagues and I have reminded hon. members that during the war of 1939-1945 spokesmen for the government time and again declared to this chamber that they would let no financial restrictions interfere with the war effort. The only thing we had to consider during wartime was whether we had the manpower and the material resources necessary for an all-out war effort. Canada did not hesitate to produce ships and guns and planes and tanks and shells to the utmost of our physical capacity; and for what? For destruction. Financial cost was of little or no concern. The government saw to it that what was physically possible was made financially possible; but they took ways of doing it that hung a millstone around the necks of the Canadian people. This is not quite one hundred per cent true, however, for I am reminded of something revealed by Professor A. F. W. Plumptre of Toronto university, who wrote an article which appeared in the Financial Post of October 5, 1940, under the title "Putting over the next war loan." I quote a brief excerpt from the article:
There are some general matters of theory which must be kept in mind in preparing for the next war loan. It must be remembered, primarily and seemingly paradoxically, that the government's object is not to get money but merely to reduce the public's spending . .	.
Then he went on:
The government can always "get money" because it may, as an alternative to borrowing or even taxation, create the required funds. This it can
The Budget-Mr. Low
easily do nowadays through the leadership of the central bank and the co-operation of the chartered banks. In this way $200 million were created in this fashion last autumn.
What for? For the war effort; not to take care of the unemployed, not to offer social security, not to close the gap between the national product and the national income, but for destructive purposes. Well, I claim that this statement, based upon facts that were brought to light in the banking and commerce committee of this house in 1939, certainly should serve to silence those critics of ours who are constantly making the assertion that the government can get money only from taxation or borrowing.
I see it is six o'clock, Mr. Speaker. I did not get started until twenty-five minutes after five, and if you would permit me just two or three minutes more I can finish.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Go ahead.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Thank you very much; I do not like to ask favours. It is clear that when Canada is faced with adverse economic conditions and the minister's tax base begins to shrink, then he ought to have the facts of the whole situation before him. He ought to know that no matter how heavily he taxes he cannot get money out of surpluses of our production that people cannot buy and use. It is only when people can buy and use goods that the minister can get taxation. That is clear. If we are to avoid economic troubles the minister will have to know exactly the relationship between the national income, which is the sum of all the money incomes of the people, and the gross national production of goods and services. He must be able to see clearly the factors and forces that are at work in our economy that produce that relationship; and he and the government need to have ready sound techniques which they can apply at once when adverse conditions begin to appear, in order to prevent further trouble.
I appeal to the government, therefore, to gather together and appoint a group of technicians, engineers, economists and businessmen. There should be not less than forty in all; have more if you wish, but forty would be able to do a good job in a reasonable time. Call them a national survey commission, or whatever you like. Charge them with the duty of investigating two main things in detail: first, the real and potential productive capacity of Canada; second, the relationship between our national income and our gross national production. These men should be kept absolutely free from political interference and they must, in my judgment, be given a free hand at all times and all the time they need to investigate fully and to
1538	HOUSE OF
Prairie Transmission Lines publicly report on the true state of affairs within this country, in the manner of the Hoover committee for the survey of potential product capacity in the United States.
I urge upon the government that they lose no time in the appointment of such a group of technicians. It is true that our economy is buoyant today; and the minister presented the other night what I thought was a buoyant and optimistic forecast for the year 1950-51. I think he was right. I think I can agree with him. But danger signs have appeared, more particularly in the United States. As I have said already, what happens in the United States to bring on adverse conditions is bound to affect our own economy. Not only that, but there are in Canada today many people on the borderline of poverty, such as pensioners, unemployables, and so on; and there are a good many too who are unemployed who could be making use of our surpluses right now. When things are buoyant, men are often too optimistic to see the danger signs until it is too late. So let us have the survey made now and the report that will be presented to us so that we can make some adequate provision for the days ahead while there is yet time to do it.
May I thank you, Mr. Speaker, for your indulgence in giving me this little bit of extra time in order to round out what I wanted to say.
At six o'clock the house took recess.
