subtopic: PRAIRIE TRANSMISSION LINES LIMITED
speechtext:
And vice versa, as the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre says. I believe that this debate has been more than justified by the information that we have obtained in the house regarding the proposed pipe lines from the oil and gas fields of Alberta to the Pacific coast.
I have listened to the arguments that have been presented by the different members for and against the different routes. I must say that the arguments have been mostly for the proposed line going through the Dominion of Canada and not down through the United States, as has been feared would be the result if these bills went through. What has impressed me most has been the attitude of the people who are most concerned in the construction of the pipe lines. I refer particularly to the legislature of British Columbia, which, as I understand, voted unanimously in favour of the pipe line going through the province of British Columbia. As all hon. members know, the legislature of British Columbia is composed of members from three different parties, namely, Conservatives, Liberals and the G.C.F., the Conservatives and the Liberals forming a coalition government and the C.C.F. the opposition. My information is that *the legislature of British Columbia voted a hundred per cent in favour of a pipe line through that province.
I have also been impressed, Mr. Speaker, by the fact that the city council of Vancouver, the city which is most interested, of course, in these pipe lines, is very much in favour of an all-Canadian route. The boards of trade of the different towns and cities throughout British Columbia, as well as labour organizations and many other bodies, have expressed the view that a pipe line, if and when constructed, should be constructed through the province of British Columbia.
As I said at the outset, these are facts, Mr. Speaker, which should impress not only the

people of western Canada, but all Canadians who are not only interested in the development of their own part of the country but anxious to see the development of the west as well as the centre and the east. If the legislature of British Columbia had voted against the pipe line going through that province, or if there had been any split in the legislature, their vote would not have been effective. If there was any great difference of opinion in these other organizations that I have mentioned then we might feel that there was some reason for a divergence or difference of opinion in this House of Commons; but such is not the case. The people who are most concerned, the people who would benefit the most, are practically unanimous in their desire that this pipe line go through the province of British Columbia.
Perhaps there was not as much interest in other parts of Canada in this pipe line a few weeks ago. That is understandable. Canada is a vast country. We in the maritime provinces, for instance, are a long way from British Columbia or' Alberta. Unless the public's attention is called to these things they do not create the interest in other sections that they do when the people learn the facts. But since this debate started I have been amazed that no matter in what part of the country you live you find that across this country today the newspapers are very much concerned and interested in this matter of the development of pipe lines in western Canada. They are very anxious that this pipe line should be constructed so that we in Canada, regardless of the part from which we come, will develop our own country first.
Some might ask, and I have been asked the question: What interest have you in New Brunswick in a line that is pumping gas in western Canada or in the western United States? Surely you have problems of your own in the maritime provinces. These are the problems which should concern you most.
We have problems. In the maritime provinces we have many problems. I have mentioned them in this house at different times, as have other hon. members from my own province and from other parts of the maritime provinces. For instance, we have oeen pressing for the Chignecto canal. We have been pressing for more hydroelectric power and for the development of the Quoddy project in New Brunswick. I have asked the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) to see if something could not be done to increase the sale of pit props in New Brunswick, which mean so much to the economy of our province and to the living conditions of our people. These are things that do concern us. But I wish to assure
Prairie Transmission Lines hon. members that we are not concerned, nor do we intend to be concerned, only with those things which are of particular interest to our section of the country.
Last night, in the few minutes I was speaking, I mentioned the fact that we are a little envious, perhaps, of the prospective prosperity-yes, and the real prosperity-of the people of Alberta and other parts of western Canada. But while we are envious we are pleased indeed that in Canada there is this great development. We believe that by developing the resources of our country, no matter what part of Canada we may come from, in that development the best interests of our country in general are being served.
This afternoon the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell), in his very excellent address on the budget, mentioned an advertisement, which he had seen in one of the papers, regarding Alberta oil. I too had seen it, and I believe it expresses the ideas regarding this development which are uppermost in the minds of many people. The advertisement says:
Alberta oil has changed his future.
By "his future" they mean the future of a young boy pictured in the advertisement. Then it goes on to say:
The boy does not know It yet. Many a grown-up does not realize it, but the new oil fields of Alberta brighten Canada's future.
There is no question about that, in western Canada, in central Canada, the whole of Canada.
Western oil is saving $100 million scarce United States dollars this year-dollars we do not have to pay out for oil imports. This means money to buy other imports we need, things which cannot be grown or made in Canada. Next year Alberta oil should save $145 million United States dollars.
Those are reasons, as I said a moment ago, that we, no matter from what part of Canada we may come, make no apology for being interested in the oil fields of Alberta, or what happens to those oil fields, or those gas fields. Then-
The search for oil is making a big, new market in Alberta ... In the prairies, petroleum product prices are lower than they would have been if oil had not been found. Prairie consumers saved more than $30 million last year. Anything that helps prairie prosperity helps all Canada.
That is good advertising-"anything that helps prairie prosperity helps all Canada". I am sure we all agree with that sentiment.
Oil is important to us all. More oil means a higher standard of living.
Then it goes on to say:
The search for oil is unending, a costly business, often disappointing; but the job is pressing forward.

Yes, they spent over $2 million, I have not the slightest doubt. They employed large crews of men for a long time.
Last year there was in the house a discussion respecting an oil pipe line. I took no part in that discussion because, for one thing, at that time I felt that it was a matter of greater concern to the western part of Canada, and to Ontario. There were a good many differences of opinion. I listened to the arguments on both sides; many convincing arguments were offered as to why the oil pipe line should go to Fort William, the home of the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Mclvor). At the same time there were quite logical arguments in favour of its going down to Superior, at the end of lake Superior. But oil is different from gas. Oil transported by pipe line can later on be shipped out in tank cars or oil tankers to other parts of the country. Gas, on the other hand, is different in
LMr. Brooks.]
that respect. Once a gas pipe line is built, the gas cannot be shipped in any other way. If the pipe line goes through the United States it means that the people of that country are the ones who will reap the benefit of having that gas. If it goes through Canada it will mean that the people of Canada or, in this instance, those of British Columbia, will benefit.
Pipe lines are today a means of transportation. We have had many different kinds of transportation in our country. First we had our rivers and canals and railways. Pipe lines are something new. Today, however, they are becoming a means of transportation. The people who pioneered in this country endeavoured to build our railways not to the north and south, so that the products of this country would be moving to the south, but rather east and west. They had vision, and built our railways east and west, so that our country would be bound together, and so that we would be a united people.
We have had some experience with building a railway to the south. The Grand Trunk was built from Montreal down to Portland, and other seaports in the state of Maine. We in New Brunswick, and the people of Nova Scotia, know what that meant to the economy of our provinces. The city of Saint John lost millions of dollars in freight charges which otherwise she would have had, if the line had not been built to Portland and other Atlantic ports of the United States. Employment was lost for thousands of longshoremen. One reason why Saint John is not larger today is that in the early days a railroad was built which siphoned off business from Quebec and other parts of Canada down into Maine and the other New England states, business that should have come to Halifax and Saint John. The same thing will happen in connection with these pipe lines if a natural resource like gas and oil is shipped into the United States rather than through Canada. The people of Canada will be the ones who will suffer.
We in the maritimes have a special interest in Saskatchewan and Alberta. Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, along with Quebec and Ontario, were the four partners in confederation in 1867. There were great open spaces in western Canada and in the regions north of Quebec and Ontario. Deals were made, one with the Hudson's Bay Company, by which this public domain was taken over by the Dominion of Canada. We in the maritime provinces helped to pay for that territory, part of which afterwards became Alberta and Saskatchewan. Other parts were added to Ontario and Quebec.

The unfortunate part is that we were the only section of Canada that did not benefit from the development that took place. Circumscribed as we were by water, it was impossible for us to expand. Great mineral resources were given to the province of Quebec when its boundaries were extended some years ago, and the same is true of Ontario. Great sections in the north were added to Saskatchewan and Alberta and it is from these sections that millions of dollars' worth of oil are being produced. As I said before, the provinces of New Brunswick and Nova Scotia helped to purchase that territory years ago and therefore we have an interest in the development that is taking place.
At times we hear what almost amounts to sneers at the suggestion of a "Canada first policy. If we were in the United States I am sure we would favour a "United States first" policy. If we were in any other country in the world we would be ready .to favour a policy that was first for that particular country. In the early days when there were few people in the country we depended upon our natural resources. We sold our furs and raw materials and our people lived from the returns of those sales. But as the country developed it was expected that there would be a similar development in manufacturing. We hoped that the raw materials would be manufactured here and that the dream of the fathers of confederation would be realized, that by 1940 we would have 40 million people in this country. Such is not the case and we may ask ourselves: Why?
It is well known that the population of any country which exports its raw materials does not grow. The people follow the raw materials. This has been true of the maritime provinces. We have been sending our raw materials to the United States and our people have followed by thousands. What is tiue of the maritime provinces is true of other parts of Canada. If you read the history of the United States before she got her independence you will find that the New England colonies got almost all their manufactured goods from Great Britain. One reason why the United States sought independence was that they wanted to manufacture in their own country. They realized that they could never build up their country as long as they bought their manufactured goods from other parts of the world, particularly from England.
The southern states have always been considered the backward states. When you ask a southerner why it is that that part of the United States has not developed as the northern part has, he will reply, "We sold our raw cotton and other raw materials to the north; our people left and we became simply hewers
Prairie Transmission Lines of wood and pickers of cotton". The great development occurred in the northern part of the country, but today the situation is being changed. Canada has suffered from the same condition of affairs. When we mention a policy of Canada first we mean that the raw materials which we have in abundance and which are today being shipped out to the value of millions of dollars should be manufactured in this country so that we can keep our people here.
The other day the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) said that we had great trade with the United States. That is true because it is only natural that two nations side by side should be great traders. But what do we find when we analyse our trade with the United States? We find that the bulk of what we ship to the United States is made up of what might be called raw materials or semi-processed goods that could have been manufactured in this country. What are the United States sending to us? Practically one hundred per cent of the imports from the United States are made up of goods that have been manufactured and perfected in that country. That is why the United States is the great, rich country she is today. As I said a moment ago, the people follow the raw materials. This has been the history of every country in the world.
As long as we persist in letting some other country take our raw materials and manufacture them, so long will the people of this country leave and go where the manufacturing industries are located. No part of Canada has suffered more in this connection than the maritime provinces. Last night the hon. member for Danforth (Mr. Harris) said that there are more Canadians in the United States than there are in Canada. There are more maritimers in and around the New England states and Boston than there are in the maritime provinces. There is hardly a family in those three provinces that has not sons and daughters or relatives in the manufacturing towns and cities of those states. We have no objection to the United States whose people are kindly, but our objective should be the same as theirs-not to build up a foreign country, but to build up our own country with our own industry and resources.
We hope that the time will come when the boys and girls of the maritimes will be able to stay in those provinces. If that is not possible I think the great majority of the people of those provinces would sooner see our boys and girls go to some other part of Canada, to Alberta and British Columbia if you will, than to the United States or some foreign country to help to build it up.

Mr. Speaker, I rise tonight to correct one or two statements that have been made, and also to reply to the hon. gentleman who has just spoken. He believes the answer to our problem lies in the hands of a committee, that all we have to do is turn it over to a committee. I should like to ask him who will eventually control the route of this pipe line. That is something I and many other hon. members would like to know. One day we had a definite, distinct statement by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) that the route is to go through Canada. Therefore we might presume that he knows about it, and in some way has control of that route. Later we were told in the house that the matter of the route must be discussed by the committee. We checked up on that and found the committee would have no power to do more than merely discuss the question of the route. Then we were told that the people who eventually would decide on the route were the board of transport commissioners; that when this application went before that board it would be accompanied by a map, on which would be delineated the route to be followed. I presume the people who made that statement were correct; but in looking over the history of our natural resources and the development that has taken place already in connection with pipe lines I find that both Saskatchewan and Alberta-and quite rightly so, from their point of view-claim they have the sole right to determine where their gas shall go and how it shall go. So if the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Mclvor) is so certain this committee can remedy the fault I would like him to prove it, because I do not see how that statement can be correct.
I believe the dominion parliament is the body that should have that control. However, we have turned it over to an appointed body who, while presumably the servants of parliament, cannot be told what to do. We cannot dictate to them; we must take their findings and hope they will work for the benefit of Canada. In other words we are discussing a matter over which we have no control or direction. We cannot change it; it is not of our making. It is not even of the government's making, and we have no choice. It is not even a matter of take it or leave it; we have to take it. We do not have the

Prairie Transmission Lines choice that the ordinary man is expected to have when he is asked to decide on anything. We have delegated our authority to others.
Previous speakers have mentioned the intense interest of British Columbia in this pipe-line bill. I can assure hon. members that in speaking to this matter I am doing so in behalf of ninety per cent of the people of that province. They are conscious of the need for this development; they are anxious to have it go through their own province. Municipal councils, boards of trade, the Canadian Legion, trade unions and all the other organized groups of that province are pleading with their members of parliament to see that this pipe line is routed through our province.
Before going further I should like to make a correction. Speaking in this house on the 14th of March I made the statement that no Canadian university offers a course in petroleum engineering. I made that statement in good faith, on the word of a United States petroleum engineer. Since then I have been corrected by someone from Alberta who is an authority on this matter, and who has drawn to my attention the fact that two years ago the university of Alberta established such a course. So far they have had no graduates, but they expect some early in the present year. I should like to compliment the university of Alberta on what they have done, and in doing so 1 should like to read a short quotation:
For the first time in the forty-five year history of Alberta as a province, a home-grown crop of petroleum engineers will be turned out into the oil industry employment market in the spring. Keeping pace with the fastest growing industry in Canada, the university of Alberta two years ago created a full degree course in petroleum engineering, the first in Canada. A group of about sixteen students will be the "charter" graduates, the class of '50.
The petroleum engineering course is the result of a couple of years of patient and painstaking research and study of curricula elsewhere in close consultation with leading representatives of all branches of the Alberta oil industry.
Then this article goes on to give reasons why they started this course. The background is that for a number of years postgraduate students from the university of Alberta who wanted to get into the oil business had been going to American universities for their post-graduate courses and, as the previous speaker said, staying there.
There were inquiries for special courses at the home university, but the university authorities did not feel that the need was sufficient for a complete petroleum course until the post-war boom in oil exploration in Alberta.
Even before the Leduc discovery, the association of professional engineers of Alberta made strong representations to the Alberta government to have a course instituted. Developments during the academic year 1946-47 made the urgency of the need apparent. The board of governors decided to
 .	.
establish a curriculum. Dean R. M. Hardy of the engineering faculty was authorized to appoint a committee of four to study and report on what was needed.
I merely refer to that in fairness to one university that is conscious of the vast wealth that is available from this great resource. At page 792 of Hansard the Minister of Trade and Commerce, replying to the hon. member for Yorkton (Mr. Stewart), said he had no knowledge of any representations from the province of Saskatchewan as far as the export of oil and gas from Alberta was concerned. I should like to point out that the first application for a gas pipe line charter from Alberta was made by Western Pipe Lines in 1948. At that time the Saskatchewan government was indirectly responsible for drawing to the attention of the house the implications of that application. In its brief to the Senate committee on transport it made the proposal that control of the lines should be given to the board of transport commissioners, and subsequently that proposal was acted upon by the federal government. That brief was printed two or three years ago, though the minister may not be aware of it. I should like to quote from it, because to my mind it is excellently prepared and in keeping with what we are trying to do today:
Few questions are of more fundamental importance to the economic life of any region than its source of heat, light and power. For this reason the government of Saskatchewan is in favour of a pipe line designed to carry natural gas across the provinces of Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba. By providing more abundant and less costly energy and fuel, the natural gas reserves of western Canada, properly developed and utilized, can prove to be a great boon to the people of the prairies.
Then it goes on to deal in detail with the Saskatchewan power commission, who presumably would take over control of'the route and service to the various towns within the province.
There is one part of the submission that I should like to place on the record, seeing that the minister is not aware of it. It is this:
Before dealing with the specific problems to which the bill gives rise, it should be indicated that the government of Saskatchewan regards the lack of a dominion statute regulating, in a general way, the activities of natural gas pipe lines, as a serious impediment to any measure of effective control of the proposed! company, in the public interest. It is difficult to import adequate principles of public control into a private bill; it is practically impossible to establish machinery capable of effecting such control in a private bill. In the opinion of the Saskatchewan government, a comprehensive dominion statute designed to regulate the activities of a public utility of the nature contemplated, is necessary if abuses are to be avoided. The United States has found federal control of interstate transportation organizations such as this to be necessary, if exploitation both of producers and consumers is to be avoided.

While there exists a sufficiently wide field for provincial control over pipe line companies operating wholly within a single province, effective control over an interprovincial pipe line is impossible without dominion participation. Conversely, the dominion acting alone lacks authority to deal effectively with the operations of such organizations. Joint legislation of a general character by the dominion and the provinces concerned, however, is capable of effecting the measures of control desirable and necessary in the public interest. The government of Saskatchewan, therefore, submits that, concurrently with the enactment of this bill, a statute, modelled upon corresponding provincial statutes and upon The Natural Gas Act of the United States, should be prepared by the dominion government and presented to parliament. At the same time, it states its own willingness to cooperate with any appropriate dominion agency for the purpose of effecting a fair and reasonable policy of direction and control in the public interest.
Rather than not having made a statement, Mr. Speaker, I claim that Saskatchewan gave an excellent lead and gave the answer to what we are seeking today, a joint control by the province and the dominion government; not by a board of transport, not by a committee, not by charters to any given company for a given route but a joint control by the province concerned and the dominion government, which we have not got and which apparently we are not seeking.

That is the only answer I have to any comment that small towns cannot consume natural gas.
We should actually concentrate on and develop the small towns in every possible way. I believe we should build our industries in the smaller towns in the interior of British Columbia rather than at the coast, particularly if there is danger of a war or if war should break out. They are too vulnerable at the coast and they would be far safer and far better protected in the interior of British Columbia. So would the population that would gather round these industries be far better protected in the interior than at the coast.
I cannot agree with any reasoning that small towns should be cut out and that large towns only justify the existence of the natural gas route. That would mean but one route through the United States. They have the large cities, whereas the number of large cities in British Columbia is limited. Possibly you could mention New Westminster, Vancouver and Victoria as centres with over
20,000	population. Beyond that, we have not many. But even so, at one time those were small towns. Even Vancouver, not many generations ago, was known as gas town, a tiny town. If the port had not been developed, if ships had not come there, if the C.P.R. had not had its terminal there, gas town would still be gas town and nothing else. I want to impress upon the members of the house the fact that we are asking them to exercise a little vision in the development of this project. Look at those little towns scattered throughout our province, with a future as great big towns such as gas town has in the modern Vancouver.
I should also like to mention one of the communities or areas in my particular riding that would benefit greatly by having this potential power or cheap power. That is the Princeton area where the mineralization is extremely high. They have practically all known minerals in abundance, such as gold, copper, silver, coal, platinum; in fact, everything. The whole area is highly mineralized. But they lack this cheap power and they lack

The Budget-Mr. Lesage it badly. Industries could be developed in connection with these metals, base metals, coal tars, dyes and so on, in that particular area quite a distance from the coast and accessible by rail to Vancouver.
One hon. member mentioned the cost to the consumer, and emphasized the fact that the extra cost of the pipe line would mean a great deal more to the consumer if it went by one route rather than another. But there is no argument there at all. To me it is a lot of hooey, because it is not a question of cost to the consumer. It is a question whether the person is going to be a consumer or not. As to the people in the interior of British Columbia, it is not a question of whether they are going to pay a dollar for a certain quantity of gas or whether they are going to pay ten dollars. The question is whether they are going to have the gas or not. That is the question we are concerned about, not the price.

The questions put by the hon. member for Moose Jaw were so put that they implied that the Quebec farmers were not paying income tax, and that Saskatchewan farmers were discriminated against by the Department of National Revenue because they were prosecuted by the income tax branch.
1 do not take exception to the figures which were mentioned in the return, and I accept them as accurate. But it is to the interpretation that one may give to those figures that we must object. Naturally, just reading the figures one would be tempted to jump to conclusions, as quickly as some have done. But it is clear that those who do jump to conclusions so quickly do not go to the bottom of the question, and do not ask themselves the reason why such a situation exists; It has always been said that comparisons are odious. Such is the case when one tries to compare the condition of the farmers of Quebec with that of Saskatchewan and the other western provinces.
Farms in Saskatchewan are cultivated on a highly commercialized or even in an industrialized way. They are very large farms, where wheat and other grains are grown, and then marketed through the pool agencies. In Saskatchewan farming is an industry: In Quebec it is a way of life. Farmers are engaged in mixed farming. Farms are relatively small, and their character is that of family organizations.
Quebec farmers have practically no employees. They work with their sons, and do not pay them wages. They keep whatever they give to them as "in trust", to buy them new farms upon which they may be established. Our farmers lead very frugal lives. Their profits and their cash income are very limited; and if they have good-looking farms it is because they have improved them with their own hands, and with the help of their families.

speechtext: Have you been in Saskatchewan and seen where farmers have homesteaded, and built up their family farms?

Yes, I have. But I shall come to figures which will show, for instance, that in 1941 there were 121,000 farmers in Saskatchewan, and 62,000 farm labourers.


That is to say, there was one farm labourer for every two farmers. In Quebec there are practically no farm labourers-practically none. In Quebec, as we shall see later, the average population per family on a farm is 5-3, while the average population per family in Saskatchewan is 3-7. I believe that is a complete answer to my hon. friend's interruption.
But let us come back to the Quebec farmer. The farmer of Quebec, as everyone knows, works from four o'clock in the morning, or perhaps five o'clock, until late at night, day in and day out. They have very few mechanized units and in some cases none. Every day they must look after their livestock. I do not believe I am exaggerating when I say -and if you have lived with them you know it is true-that if success is to be achieved it must be as the result of the co-operative efforts of the family unit.
Let us come back to the figures obtained by the hon. member for Moose Jaw, in his return. Those figures, I suggest, show that only a small number of Quebec farmers paid income tax in 1947. I believe the figure is 540.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Very successful.

Wait until you hear the figures, and then you will know why more did not pay.
I repeat, one must know the conditions of the farmers in Quebec before intimating that practically all of them are trying to escape, or are in fact escaping from the provisions of the income tax law, or that they are receiving more favourable treatment from the taxing authorities.
Now, listen to the figures, because they speak for themselves:	The total number of
farmers in Quebec in 1941 stood at 131,406. This number, according to the information I gathered from the provincial department of agriculture in Quebec, has increased. One hon. member has said that the number of farmers in Quebec in 1947 was 155,000. I do not know, and I suggest no one knows, the exact figure. But I believe that that figure is a little high. It will be noticed, however, as I go along, that for the purposes of my calculation the higher the figure the more it will serve my case. So, for the sake of argument, let us say that the number in 1947 was approximately 140,000. Now, the net ' farm income of the province of Quebec in 1947, according to the dominion bureau of statistics, was $190,300,000. If one divides that income by the number of farmers, taking the figure at approximately 140,000, one will find that the average net income in Quebec for the farmer, in 1947, was $1,350.

I do not wish to have anyone believe that I imply that Quebec farmers live in a state of poverty. One must take into consideration the fact that in Quebec the farm is a family enterprise, and that Quebec farmers work steadily and maintain their farms by their own personal work, and by the work of their families.
Their cash income is very limited; I repeat that. One may refer to their prosperous dairy industry. Well, that is all very well for the western farmer; but one should hear the complaints made by eastern farmers-not only those of Quebec, but those of eastern Ontario-about the price of feed grains from the west.
I am serious in saying that if the federal government had not paid a subsidy on transportation costs, not only would those eastern farmers obtain no profit from their dairy industry, but they would spend on it profits coming from other sources. The work done by the Quebec farmer engaged in the dairy industry provides no profit, but gives him an hourly wage that no labourer would accept. This is all due to the cost of production, in which one of the main items is the very high price of feed grains which come, alas! for the Quebec farmer, at a high cost, but which give to the western farmer some of the profits the eastern farmer should expect from his dairy farm.
Let us return to the figures I have before me. I said the average net income of the Quebec farmer was $1,350 per year. In 1947 the income  tax exemption for a married couple was $1,500. For a married man with three children of family allowance age the exemption was $1,800. For a man with three children, one over sixteen years and two of family allowance age, the exemption was $2,000. I repeat that the average rural family in Quebec is 5'3 persons. How could anyone expect the Quebec farmer to be subject to income tax in 1947 when his average exemption was around and above $2,000 with an average net income of about $1,350? With the figures I have given I think it will be agreed that the great majority of Quebec farmers do not have to file income tax returns because it is taken for granted, and rightly so, that they are not liable to income tax.
It should not be said that the Quebec farmers have not been investigated by the Department of National Revenue. The contrary is the case. The inspectors of the department visited the secretary-treasurers of the municipalities of Quebec and examined the books which showed the value of the farms in the municipalities. They inquired about the value of the cattle and the farms and when those values were a certain figure
The Budget-Mr. Lesage the farmers were asked to file returns. They did so with very few exceptions. A great proportion of the farmers who did file returns were able to show quite easily that they were not subject to income tax. When it became evident to the inspector of the department that these farmers with their small income and numerous dependents were not subject to the tax their names were taken off the tax roll. That was the only sensible thing to do especially when one considers that since 1946 exemptions have been increased three times.
I am not saying that the Quebec farmer lives in a state of poverty, but I repeat that he lives a frugal life. He is richer in courage than in cash income. I would be only too glad, and I am sure the Quebec farmers would be quite satisfied, if their income were raised to such an extent that practically all had to pay an income tax. If some hon. members of this house knew what I know of their condition they would be the last ones to contend that the farmers of Quebec have received special treatment in this regard.
Without making any undue comparison, let me turn now to the Saskatchewan farmer. As I have said already, the farms in Saskatchewan are highly commercialized and industrialized.

115,000	which I have just mentioned, paid income tax in that year. With all due respect

My hon. friend, as we say in French, "a perdu une belle occasion de se taire", because he has taken on his own shoulders the responsibility of proving- with my help of course-first, that there is nothing extraordinary in the fact that only a few Quebec farmers had to pay income tax in 1947 and, secondly, that it was the duty of the Department of National Revenue to see that more Saskatchewan farmers paid their taxes.
Of course, I would not like the Saskatchewan farmers to believe that I have anything against them because the contrary is the fact. subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to address the house on the budget which was recently delivered because I believe the budget speech is the principal message by the government to the people in


all walks of life and to industry as to how they should govern themselves for the years to come. I take a little different view on the amount of the budget, $2,430 million, than other hon. members. I would have been a little more pleased if the government had been going to spend $3 billion. The surplus of some $20 million would not have bothered me so much if I did not look back on the 1930's when world-wide developments affected the ordinary course of business in such a way that a surplus of $20 million would soon be eaten up.
In this undeveloped tremendously rich country, with a cabinet selected from a party which has the largest percentage of members that the House of Commons has ever known, the cabinet 'ministers are supposed to head individual departments such as agriculture, finance, trade and commerce, health, railways and immigration. The cabinet meets months before the budget is actually read by the Minister of Finance for the information of the people of Canada as a whole. Upon the decision of the cabinet as to the path they are going to follow and the light they are going to hold before the people of Canada, the amount of the budget is settled.
In the budget speech-and I studied it very carefully-there was not the slightest suggestion that the government of Canada should spend more money than they are now and still have a reduction in taxation and the cost of living. The bureau of statistics of the Dominion of Canada, under the control of the cabinet ministers of the government, has a better knowledge than anybody of the figures concerning the development of the iron ore of Labrador and Quebec and the development of oil and natural gas in the province of Alberta. There is no group of people in Canada that should know the potentialities of the development of the country in the next twelve months better than the cabinet.
The budget speech is the green light tor everybody. Manufacturers and industrialists all wait for it. On the basis of it the hardheaded developers of Canada decide what they should do in the coming twelve months. There was no enlightenment in the budget as to what any industry should do. There was nothing to guide them whether they should expand or curtail. There is no relief for the workingman who pays taxes, and there is no relief from the high cost of living. There can be no doubt or dispute that these things are clearly indicated by the budget presented to the people of Canada by the Minister of Finance.
It is almost time for the people of Canada to make up their minds whether we are going

to develop this country as a nation or whether we are going to become a part of the United States. From the actions of the government, and their lack of foresight and guidance as clearly depicted in the budget, we are heading in the direction of continuing to permit the development of our iron ore and natural gas and oil by United States interests. If we stop to reflect we will realize that the International Nickel Company is controlled by the United States, as is the American Can Company, Palmolive Soap Company and all of the automotive industry. All the leading oil companies of the Dominion of Canada are controlled today by the United States, and the kind of news we are constantly getting is United States financed, United States controlled.
The premier of Newfoundland held back the good news when he was bubbling over to tell what a great job some Canadians had done, that they had been successful in making available millions of dollars for the purchase and control of the assets of Canada by United States interests. In a recent newspaper article there is the following:
Price increases ranging from one-tenth to three-fifths of a cent on various oil products were announced for eastern Canada . . .
They were announced by Imperial Oil. I believe that the members of the cabinet are endowed with enough intelligence to get down to common sense. Each cabinet minister should send out word that we are going to start to develop Canada, that we are going to increase our annual budget, and that we are going to decrease taxation. There is no mystery about that procedure. There is only one method of increasing your budget, and that is by taking more money from fewer people. The people who have more money should pay more than they have paid, in previous years. At the same time the high cost of living would be reduced and we would be letting money remain in the pockets of Canadians so that they would have something to save over and above providing for the bare necessities of life.
I believe I am safe in saying that at the present time Canada is the greatest and wealthiest undeveloped country in the world, but who holds the reins? The people who have vision, the industrialists of Canada, are having their vision and desires curtailed because the budget would exercise a restraining influence on any wise-thinking board of directors. There is no reduction in taxation and we have a budget of $2,430 million. It seems that the position of the government is one of wait and see and pray to the Almighty that something will arise such as a war to bring about prosperity. I may be wrong, but I believe every member elected to the House of Commons is
The Budget-Mr. Ferguson elected because his constituents believe that he will contribute something towards the government of Canada by way of guidance and aid.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is what happened last year.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Of course that could be expected. It was anticipated before you arrived here because we knew there was an election coming in June. That was not news to the public; it was a foregone conclusion. That will always happen with a Liberal government prior to an election. Don't worry about that. When an election will not take place until four years from now the government reverts to its true form and a position of wait and see and pray to the Almighty. They take the position that we will not develop the resources of Canada, that we will continue to burden the people, that the people can tighten their belts and do without things they want but do not necessarily need. Nevertheless they want them just the same. This Liberal government says that there will be no reduction in taxation but that we will have social services. I am not advocating the curtailment of any social services. I wish I had more time; I would advocate greater social services.
There is a shipyard in the town of Colling-wood, where I live, which has produced some of the finest boats ever built. That shipyard produced the largest freighter ever built on the great lakes in peacetime, as well as the largest passenger boat. It produced some of the finest ships of war when called upon to do so in the two world wars. The men working there are willing and able workers, but what is their prospect today?. They have one oil tanker to build, and nothing else in sight. There has been a continual reduction of staff. They are faced with the possibility that they may have to leave the homes they have endeavoured to pay for over a period of twenty years. This may bring smiles to the faces of some of the Liberal members of this house, but the situation is serious for the welder, the riveter or the labourer in the shipyard, who returned to work only last month after living for four months on unemployment insurance. There is nothing to smirk at in a situation like that.
I am here to suggest and not to meanly criticize. This government, which has men such as the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Fournier) and others with great ability, certainly should be able to do something about the present situation. It may be necessary to issue bonds for certain national projects that will conserve our wealth, assure employment and cause immigration to come into this country. Surely we Canadians are sick and

The Budget-Mr. Ferguson tired of seeing a province like Saskatchewan with only seven or eight hundred thousand people, Alberta with about eight hundred thousand, Ontario with four million, Quebec with three and a half or four million, and a total population in this vast country, of only fourteen million. To the south we have a country of 150 million. That population did not get there through the wave of a wand. It is true that we have certain climatic handicaps they do not have; but offsetting our cold winter months we have riches untold which they do not have. But we leave them undeveloped, or wait for the Americans to develop them, and permit them to keep the reins in their hands.
I beseech the members of the cabinet to be fairer in their dealings with this house. Let them ask, "What must we do?" We should build a great nation here. We should treble our population, so that in the years to come taxation will be less on the individual and the small businessman. Look at the tremendous growth in our industry and natural resources caused by a war. Why should it be left to a war to bring about these developments? Cannot the men who are in positions of responsibility give the people of Canada a feeling of confidence, so that industrialists will say, "We are prepared to spend more money to expand our industries." The government will be able then to bring in bigger budgets than ever, with far less taxation on the individual person or firm.
I have mentioned a few industries that take most of the cream of our efforts out of this country. Do people stop to consider that annually millions of dollars go from this country to England in reinsurance, in premiums paid by the taxpayers of Canada? Not long ago I noticed the financial statement of a prominent United States insurance company which has several branches in Canada. It has invested in bonds of its own government some $45 million, while it has only a little more than $1 million in Canadian government bonds. The competition is so great that something must be done by this government. It is a bitter pill to swallow, but it is a fact that in the past, through subservience and necessity, much of the fruits of our labour went to other countries. Now Canadians find themselves in the position that something must be done to encourage Canadian capital to invest in our own country and develop our natural resources.	[DOT]
Let me give one example of what I mean. No ship can ply the coastal waters of the United States unless it was built in that country. What is the situation in Canada? About seventy per cent of the ships of Canadian registry plying our coastal waters were constructed in foreign countries. A Canadian


company can go to the United States, purchase a boat, bring it to Canada and operate it in our coastal waters; but our generous friends to the south have a sweet little law which says that no company there may buy a boat built in Canada and operate it in their United States water. How much longer must we wait before taking similar measures to develop our own country?
In a way I hate to see the government interfering with any business. I am not speaking only of this government; but from what I have seen in the past of governments, provincial and federal, they have made a holy mess of everything they have ever tackled in the line of business. Today, however, the situation is so grave that something must be done. The cabinet ministers of this government have had experience which should put them far ahead of any of their predecessors, as a group. So they should not skirt this problem, or close their eyes to it; they should recognize the problem and come to grips with it.
In his budget speech the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) declared, "This is the budget. There is no relief." In other words he practically said, "I don't know what to do about it. Let us see what the outcome will be." That might be all right if we had reached the point where we had nothing more to develop. That might be all right if we had a population of 180 million people and did not have to rely upon export markets; but that is not all right with conditions as they are today. People pay $160 for a washing machine in Canada while the same machine sells in the United States for $60. We pay a third more for an automobile produced in this country than the same vehicle costs in the United States. The day may come when we have automobiles at a greater percentage per population than we have today, when we are able to buy these commodities with a certain degree of ease, and when the householders no longer look in the shop windows for twenty years and say, "My, wouldn't I like to own an automatic washing machine, but I can't afford it. The grocery bill, the meat bill, my rent, my clothing, take all I can possibly make. I must continue to break my back over an old-type washing machine." Or else pay, with eyes closed to the insurance premiums to protect the family in case of death, with eyes closed on the proper education of our children, buying a washing machine at a Canadian price which is ridiculous only owing to the fact that we have not a market in Canada to compare with the United States.
There is something radically wrong that we here find ourselves with fourteen million

people. There is no necessity for that. I do not advocate indiscriminate immigration; but the planners, the developers of Canada, who are the great private industries, should receive guidance from this government so that they will be compelled to bring additional labour from Europe in order to cope with the growing pains and the growth of Canada due to the development of natural resources and industry.
I think back thirty years, and each year I have hoped that Canadians would be able to receive, for the same effort and the same intelligence, approximately the same remuneration for their services as they would receive in the United States. But we continue here, year after year, to take as a foregone conclusion what is happening, and the stream of some of the finest boys and girls this country ever has raised continues annually to pour down into the United States-

speechtext:
-where they will receive better compensation for their efforts. The statement that the stream continues will not tolerate any degree of accurate contradiction. That has been the case for years. Furthermore, there are hundreds of people in Canada who have to face the deplorable fact that, for the sake of receiving better money, they would like to go to the United States but they cannot go. Only recently a sailor in my home town asked that I help him get across the border. I said that it could not be done legally, that the Americans would not stand for it. He informed me that he would receive almost double the money in the United States, working on the same type of ship, the same type of cargo and over the same route on the great lakes. How much longer must we be satisfied with that situation? How much longer must we look at our children coming along and say, "Well, that is your cake from Canada. That is all you can look forward to." How ridiculous that is. If the government of Canada as a body would go over this country from coast to coast, would give up golf games, five o'clock teas, public receptions and political speeches and get right down to earth -yes, a little less running around the world and a little more examination of the undeveloped wealth of Canada-I believe we would have had a different budget from the one we have just had presented to us. You cannot be too emphatic about this situation. We are all here to help Canada. I am not maliciously or meanly criticizing this government. I am asking that something be done in the next twelve months, that whoever the minister of finance may be, he give out the sweet music to everybody's ears, "Your taxes have been reduced."
The Budget-Mr. Major
The budget is greater than ever before; the wealth of the country has expanded, making this possible. Surely the members of the Liberal party here in this house tonight cannot sit back and seriously say that they are satisfied with the budget speech which the people of Canada have to tolerate, the most uninformative speech ever delivered in the house. It was purely a case of "That is the money we need to run the country, and you can go on sweating and expect to receive the same paltry compensation that you have been receiving in the past"; and there will be no guidance from this government as to what we may expect in the future, how big our industries should grow within the next twelve months or four or five years.
A few nights ago I heard one man here make a statement with regard to the pipe line that is to be used in western Canada. He said that the Steel Company of Canada could make this steel pipe. The Steel Company of Canada, by the way, is owned by United States Steel. They have their hands on all the steel in the country. There is no doubt about that. This member of the house said it would cost $5 million to create that steel. What of it? This government should have been whispering in the ear of the Steel Company "Go ahead; we expect we shall be utilizing half a billion dollars' worth of steel at least." If the groundwork to produce this steel is going to cost $5 million, it is a mere fleabite when you consider that the money will all remain in Canada. It will be here to be used by Canadians. It will be here to develop Canada. Please let us have some semblance of encouragement so that Canadians will develop Canada, so that they will be relieved of excessive and unnecessary taxation, and so that the Dominion of Canada will be in a position to spend a far greater sum on its budget than it ever spent in its history before. Canada can stand it and so can Canadians.

I did not
intend to speak on the budget, Mr. Speaker, but a matter of urgent importance to the farmers of eastern Ontario prompts me to avail myself of this opportunity to speak briefly, as the occasion may not again be available until after the Easter recess.
At this time the farmers are greatly disturbed over the abrupt increase in the price of grain they have to buy from western Canada. Feed wheat which was costing the farmer of my constituency $3.45 per hundred pounds on January 1, 1950, is now sold to him at $3.75 per hundred pounds or $2.25 per bushel, an increase of 8 per cent since January 1. Feed oats which was costing the farmer
1554	HOUSE OF COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. Bruneau $2.75 per hundred pounds on January 1, 1950, is now being sold to him at $3.70 per hundred pounds or $1.25 per bushel, an increase of 95 cents per hundred pounds, or 35 per cent since January 1, 1950.
These prices which I have just quoted are the prices that I, as a farmer, had to pay for grain delivered to me by my dealer. I am sure that there is no reason for this abrupt increase in the price of grain to the eastern Ontario farmer at this time, and it should be re-established at normal price immediately.
While the price of wheat is up 8 per cent, oats 35 per cent and feed rations accordingly, it must be remembered that cheese, hogs, and eggs have been reduced by 10 per cent.
Considering the increase in the price of grains and the decrease in the price that the farmer must take for his various farm products, you may be assured that he will be unable to pay this increased grain price and that he will be forced to discontinue the purchase of feed.
This in turn will mean decreased production to meet our cheese and bacon contracts and a still lesser production to meet what may be a seriously low supply of eggs this fall and followed with all its reaction to the consumer.
The fact that the farmer will be forced to discontinue his purchases of feed may also cause accumulated feed to remain in western Canada-a condition which I am sure our western farmers would not like to see created.
I know of only two ways to remedy this condition, Mr. Speaker: one would be the immediate reduction of the price of grain and the other an increase in the support price to offset the increase in grain price. Which shall it be?	[DOT]

Mr. Speaker, as the representative of a rural constituency where the majority of the electors belong to the farming class, I consider it my duty tonight, while debating on the budget under study at the present time, to congratulate this government on the passing of a bill in support of farm prices. In doing so, I have the sincere feeling that we are helping those who, through their work, endeavour and efforts, are striving towards achieving the development and progress of our country.
For quite a number of years now, cost of living bonuses have been granted to various working classes, but as yet no bonus has ever been allotted to the farmers except through this price support policy, and I believe it to be an essential one.
If we are to avoid unemployment and a standstill in industry, let us afford the man of the field the opportunity to sell at a decent

price. In this way we shall enable him to buy commodities and in doing so, enable the working class, the workman his brother, to produce the current commodities of life. As I stated at a meeting in Plantagenet, in my constituency of Prescott, some time ago, I will pledge myself to support any measure that will help our farming class. By thus ensuring their welfare we shall also ensure that of the labouring class and so promote that true prosperity towards which we all aspire.
I firmly believe, sir, that a good portion of the estimates in the budget under review will be well spent if it is directed in greater measure towards the implementation of the agricultural price-support policy.
I believe also that a great majority of the people of my constituency, and those of the neighbouring ridings, would welcome any estimates from the Department of Public Works which would be used in curbing the waters of one of the wickedest rivers in Canada, the Nation river.
Last Sunday afternoon I was invited to a meeting in St. Isidore de Prescott situated in the southwestern tip of my constituency, but at some distance past Plantagenet. Instead of rolling farm lands, there was a lake in front of me. The Nation river was flooding again. I hope that the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Fournier) will see that some of the estimates of his department are well spent on irrigation works or whatever program will enable the curbing of this yearly flood; and I hope that I shall not miss another annual meeting in that region because of the overflowing of that river.
While contemplating the possibilities of this budget, I would also like, in common with many colleagues in this house, to see the introduction in our social security program of a system of allowances to every person, without any sufficient income or means of support who, by reason of an injury, accident, congenital infirmity or incurable disease, is at a disadvantage in seeking or obtaining employment, or incapable of providing for his subsistence, and whose age prevents him from benefiting from the social security legislation now in force. Such a system is already proposed in a resolution tabled in this house. I believe a large percentage of the problems which are presented to the representatives of the people are those created by. circumstances facing such handicapped persons and I am sure, Mr. Speaker, that any legislation to that effect would certainly mean estimates well spent in our budget.
Should we also have an excess of money which we are not too sure what to do with, I wish to inform you, Mr. Speaker, that a

theatre group known as "Le Cercle Gascon", in my home town of Hawkesbury, recently won the Le Droit trophy in the recent dramatic festival held in Hull, last March 18, and it might have to compete in a coming dominion drama festival to be held in Calgary. A trip there would cost about $2,000.
I	believe it would be quite an encouragement to theatrical activities in Canada.
Such are the objectives I would like to see realized under the budget for the fiscal year 1950-51, and I am sure I voice here the views of a good majority of the members in this house.
