speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising for the first time to speak in this house, I deem it my duty at the outset to express the gratefulness of my constituents to the present government and especially to its leader-my leader-from whom it has received such competent and distinguished leadership. Indeed, the constituency of Lapointe did not exist prior to 1947.
The Representation Act, 1947, chapter 71,
II	George VI, states:
Lapointe, consisting of the city of Arvida and the towns of Kenogami and Jonquifere, together with that part of the county of Chicoutimi situated west of the western limits of the townships of Gagne, Tremblay, Chicoutimi, Laterriere, the western part of the townships of Lartigue and Lapointe situated west of the Boisvert river (Cyriac) together with the whole territory situated north of the townships of Falardeau, Begin, Labrecque, and west of a meridian line passing through the northeast angle of the township of Falardeau.
Such is the legal or detailed description, if I may use that term, of my constituency.
In fact, our section of the country has been most richly endowed by nature. Although relatively young-Jonquiere, the mother city of Kenogami and Arvida, was founded a little over a hundred years ago-our section of the province of Quebec is still one of the most important. Our unrivalled water power and basic industries have transformed my constituency into one of the vital parts of Canada. But above all our population is worthy of admiration. French-Canadian traditions that have been lauded, and rightly so, by historians, travellers and all those who have observed us objectively, have been fully preserved in my constituency.
Nowhere else in the country, though it is the size of a continent, have the working classes and the farm population shown a better spirit and a clearer understanding of their rights and obligations, done their duty in a more intelligent fashion or claimed their rights with more tranquil assurance.
The Budget-Mr. J. Gauthier
Our constituency can also set an example in other respects. Some of my electors, for instance, are English-speaking; yet I can state without fear of contradiction that, among us, no problems spring from racial or religious antagonism. Everyone lives in an atmosphere that has not been tainted by petty, narrow nationalism. Yet, our national life, in the best sense of the term, has had intensive development and flourishes in the best Canadian soil. Our relations are based on the respect of mutual rights. Commendable emulation exists among our French- and English-speaking fellow citizens. That is the keystone of our relations. I am therefore especially proud to mention it and to tender an invitation to those who wish to see how concrete action and achievements can be brought about in peace and harmony.
My love for truth, as well as my love for "my little country" and its incomparable people, compelled me to point out this state of affairs.
From the "management-labour" angle, many particular achievements and viewpoints should be drawn to the attention of the house.
We live in the centre of the aluminum industry, a fact known to all. As a matter of fact, one can find in Arvida the largest aluminum factory in the world, where aluminum is produced through the hydroelectric developments at Chute-a-Caron and Shipshaw, which produce more than a million horsepower and remain one of the most daring feats of engineering. I would be remiss in my duty if I failed to point out the leading part played by the Arvida plants during the second world war. The war material we supplied to the Canadian air force, as well as that of the United States and of our allies in general, became an essential element of victory. And in order to pay tribute to those concerned, I must mention a few names.
Had it not been for the leadership and boundless energy of one R. E. Powell and his immediate assistants, Messrs. J. B. White, Lamountain, Whittaker, Johnson and Farrell, we would have been much longer in achieving victory in the field. These men have shown themselves to be, not only great industrial leaders, but craftsmen to whom-it may be said without exaggeration-the allied nations as well as Canada are greatly indebted.
Our military leaders have been shown the gratitude they were entitled to and I associate myself wholeheartedly with all the words of praise which have been showered
1556	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. J. Gauthier upon them. But not enough has been said,
I think, of the tremendous task accomplished by our industrial leaders with the help of their faithful workers. To my mind, their names should be inscribed upon the honour roll of our nation.
Mr. Speaker, in paying tribute to the people of my constituency and to the essential role they have played during the war,
I have obeyed no chauvinistic dictates. Besides, there are other reasons for calling Arvida a model city. Recently this progressive community won first place in fire prevention work throughout this country. On that occasion it was my privilege and pleasure to congratulate once more its officials whose efforts enabled our town to achieve top ranking in every field.
If I talk somewhat at length about our industries and our manufacturers I do so with pleasure and I know that all the people I represent will thank me for it.
Back home friendly relations between employees and employers are an old tradition. Management and workers have always looked upon each other as friends and fellow workers. If such a feeling prevails there it is due to a very large extent to the Price family who have set up their plants and their main industries at Jonquiere and Kenogami. When you talk about the Price people in the region you are bound to please all who have known the humble beginnings of that part of the country and its stupendous development. These employers were not satisfied to use honestly acquired capital and make it grow but they considered their employees as members of a family who, although their immediate interests are sometimes different, must work towards a common goal: the welfare of a hard-working people filled with the ambition and the legitimate pride to reach the top level in their particular activities.
My tribute to the two great industries located in my riding should arouse no suspicion; I have spoken nothing but the absolute truth. Private enterprise in its soundest aspects shall always find in me a true and reliable supporter. I do not fear to make that statement to the country at large.
In 1943, as mayor of the city of Jonquiere, I was chosen by the workers as their spokesman and mediator in the strikes at the Price plants. They showed me their gratitude for having championed their cause by entrusting me with the more important mandate of member for the riding of Lapointe. I may say quite frankly and quite honestly that the Price Company is conscious not only of its responsibilities in equity but also of its social respon-


sibilities towards its employees; the latter, on the other hand, besides being good technicians, are fully aware of all the responsibilities of the modern worker.
Unfortunately, Mr. Speaker, what I have to say is not all pleasant. Our country is immense. In size, it is a whole continent. It has intricate problems. During the war, thanks to the Liberal government, friction and internal strife were reduced to a minimum. I make this statement with a certain amount of pride since our country has been one of the few belligerent countries to retain a party government. This is undoubtedly due to the fact that we had a truly honest government and that the Liberal party became identified with the spirit which inspires any nation in those solemn hours when its very future is at stake.	.
We have had government controls. The wartime prices and trade board has not only proven- useful but it has won the admiration of many other countries. Why? Chiefly because its initial purpose was to serve public interest. In view of the shortcomings of human nature it was necessary to curb exaggerated profits, to protect the masses against abuses which, although understandable, are nevertheless objectionable. It was necessary to combine a sound, energetic, fearless and untainted control with free enterprise, the basis of our democratic system. We have had the wartime prices and trade board. It has exercised in fact an efficient control and the Liberal party deserves the credit.
By the way, may I congratulate my leader and the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) on the appointment of Mr. Gordon as president of the Canadian National Railways. That is, on Canada's part, an act of justice and of gratitude to a leading servant who will henceforth perform his duties with a foremost organization, that is our national system of railways. There is a man appointed to a job that was meant for him.
In my constituency, however, the wartime prices and trade board has made what I still consider a mistake. I point it out with the same frankness which has marked my preceding remarks.
During the summer of 1949, the rental division of the wartime prices and trade board decided to decontrol houses belonging to the Aluminum Company of Arvida. As a result, over 1,000 tenants in the city of Arvida had to pay substantial increases in rent. That step was unfair and unwarranted. At the

time I drew the matter to the attention of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott). I was not the only one to express that opinion.
The election campaign was in full swing when we heard the surprising and strange news that rental accommodation was being decontrolled at Arvida. Mr. Lobley had taken that decision. After consulting my advisers, I concluded that such a step could not be justified. Controls could not so suddenly become objectionable. If they had been proved ineffective, why were they being abandoned at Arvida only?
Everyone must bear his own responsibilities. Nobody will convince me that at Arvidji rents should be tied to wages and that rents had also been decontrolled in other places where houses belonged to employers. At that time, a large number of property owners were in the same situation but they continued to come under government control.
In this respect, I made representations to the Minister of Finance but I am sorry to say that justice has not been done to Arvida tenants.
I do not claim that the rents paid the owners were adequate. I commend the Aluminum Company for having provided this housing accommodation at low rates which were insufficient in many cases. However, while other landlords in the same position were subject to rent control, those at Arvida were not affected by it and tenants of that city had to take the consequences. I point out to the Minister of Finance that I have not changed my mind. I believe that full justice, democratic and liberal justice, has not been done my constituents in Arvida.
I do not wish to involve anyone, but just the same it should be pointed out that the arbitrary course taken by Mr. Lobley, rental controls administrator, also surprised and astonished the hon. member for Outremont (Mr. Rinfret). As a matter of fact, the hon. Postmaster General gave me his unequivocal support during my electoral campaign when a rather bitter discussion took place at Arvida on rental controls. I thank him.
When my leader announced that the hon. Postmaster General had become a member of the government, I was delighted to hear of his appointment, which he had more than deserved. I was proud to have been supported by such a man and I want to express my sincere gratitude to him.
The Budget-Mr. J. Gauthier
Now, in any event, I formally repeat my wish that full justice should be given to my constituents in Arvida.
This is how the member for Lapointe constituency respects the promise made to his constituents and electors. Fearlessly, he claims from the house what he promised his constituents and he draws to the particular attention of his respected leader, of the right hon. the Minister of Finance and of the Right Hon. Mr. Howe this matter of national importance, since it is a matter of principle and justice.
Mr. Speaker, during the last session of parliament, my distinguished colleague, Mr. Andre Gauthier, member for Lake St. John, called the attention of this house and of the government to the fact that lumberjacks were not entitled to unemployment insurance benefits.
I wish to congratulate my hon. friend for this timely gesture, which may be found recorded in Hansard for October 25, 1949, at page 1144. Since then, the government has carried out the recommendations of my colleague from Lake St. John, which goes to show that from within the Liberal party may come suggestions towards the common good to which the government is ready to subscribe. I ask the Prime Minister and his distinguished colleagues to accept my personal thanks, as well as those of the electors of the constituency of Lapointe, among whom may be found several hundred lumberjacks, as well as the thanks of those who are of one mind with the member for Lake St. John and myself.
Mr. Speaker, I am firmly convinced that any suggestion, any recommendation, offered in this house in the interests of the people will' be acted upon by the government if it can be carried out. That is why I unhesitatingly suggest to the leaders of this country what I consider to be the policy to be followed with respect to old age pensions.
Inasmuch as industry and commerce obey the law of nature,-at least I hope they do,- they will not keep at work people who have reached 65 years of age. Personally, I am of the opinion that one is not disabled at this age but that, on the contrary, one can make one's employer profit by the intangible asset of experience, in addition to one's work. However, facts are facts and industry mercilessly lays off workers who have reached 65 years of age. That is the fateful age, the age which puts an end to a man's work but unfortunately does not put an end to his needs. They may not be as great as during the two or three preceding decades, but they still exist. Under our system, which is not faultless, but which we must accept with its
1558	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. J. Gauthier advantages and deficiencies, it is the duty of the state to help wage earners when they reach the age of 65. I wish to make the following proposals:
1.	At 65, every Canadian citizen should be entitled to an old age pension, the amount of which shall be in relation with the cost of living, after an investigation has proved the need of such pension.
2.	Old age pensions should be paid automatically at the age of 70, to any person, man or woman.
My proposals have been carefully thought out and are the result of experience. My constituents belong to the working class. I solemnly declare to the government of this country, my government, that it is unfair, in my opinion, that working people should have to eke out a living and be the prey of anxiety, uncertainty and unhappiness for a period of five years, from 65 to 70.
Though I am a member of parliament, I do not forget that I have been and remain a notary. In that capacity, I can state that many people prematurely dispossess themselves of their property in order to get, once they reach 70, the old age pension on the basis it is paid at present in this country. As a result, the situation is, in many cases, abnormal. I believe it would be sound administrative policy on the part of the government to grant old age pensions to people 70 years old without the means test; in this way family allowances are paid, just as the sun, which is good in itself, sheds its beneficial rays irrespective of the merits of the recipients.
These ideas should surprise no one. In 1950, we no longer argue as we did in 1900 or 1867. I know that truth is eternal and unalterable. However, the relative truths encountered in administrative measures cannot be compared to absolute truth. They must adapt themselves to special needs and to various periods. Moreover, is it not the privilege of Liberalism to develop itself constantly? Its evolution, though, must be progressive and based on nothing but the possible and practicable happiness of the masses who know how to condition their rights by relating them to their duties.
Could it be that there are people who consider my remarks to be too bold? They do not know my leader. And they are not true Liberals since, essentially, it is the duty of a Liberal to honestly express a fair and honest thought, unmindful whether it runs counter to interests which, legitimate though they may be, are nonetheless private interests.
[Mr Gauthier (Lapointe).]

If I should be called upon to give a concrete example of my love for freedom of thought and speech, I would say that radical reforms should be made in the way our penal laws are enforced. I would say that a cause as worthy, just and reasonable as that which the Montreal Le Devoir has just espoused, with respect to public morals, should gain the support of public opinion and honest folk. When evidence is offered to the intelligence of common people and leading citizens alike that brings them to the necessary and objective conclusion that all is not well, that law-abiding people are not adequately protected, that the conscience of honest men cries for vengeance, I cannot but say and no one will prevent me from saying that morality laws are ill enforced, inasmuch as in a dispute which has arisen between leaders legally and legitimately chosen to do good- here again, is it these so called authorities that-but I do not care to mention the reasons

should prevent them from uniting for the eradication of evil?
Our Criminal Code must be enforced to the full, municipal police forces must co-operate to this end with provincial and federal forces and not remain inactive because of a jurisdictional dispute.
This brings me to express a few simple home truths, unpleasant though they may be.
Politics or, to be more exact, politicians are doing great damage to our country generally and, more particularly, to our beloved province of Quebec. A political dictatorship, organized or at least encouraged covertly by the provincial government of that province, is spreading its tentacles in the municipal, school administration and even parochial fields. This attitude robs life of its flavour and, in some cases, poisons it entirely.
It is more than ever high time to call a halt to our fratricidal struggles, as Mercier once did. However, peace must be achieved with dignity and not by surrendering unconditionally to an arbitrary power which, having menaced public order, seeks also the total and absolute ruin of those who, in good faith, and following the dictates of justice and reason, have fought against it and continue to do so.
Mr. Speaker, at the beginning of my speech I spoke about my constituency and my constituents, a subject naturally more pleasant than my last remarks.
Fortunately I have reserved these last moments to talk about my revered leader, the Right Hon. Louis St. Laurent. First of all I want to thank him for having chosen

as Deputy Speaker of the house a man as distinguished as the hon. member for Roberval, who is to a certain extent my political godfather. The county of Lapointe, the name of which recalls both Mgr. Eugene Lapointe and his namesake the former Minister of Justice, owes to him-at least to a great extent

its existence as a distinct unit. In that regard, I want to say that the Saguenay people were particularly happy to hear of the admission to the cabinet of the Hon. Hugues Lapointe. He fought with valour on the battlefields and the people in the county that bears his name rely on him also to uphold, in the councils of the nation, the democratic ideals which were, are and will remain common to the illustrious minister of justice that was Ernest Lapointe, to our distinguished and beloved Solicitor General, and to the modest but sincere member for Lapointe.
Great tasks await the Solicitor General and we can rest assured of his success just as he can count on our co-operation. I wish to thank him in particular for the gracious way in which he has received a delegation from Saguenay, which had come to acquaint him with the needs of our unemployed.
I know the government has done a great deal for our people. Unemployment insurance has shown that it was not only useful but necessary. More will have to be done, however.
As far as I am concerned, I have already had the privilege, as mayor of the city of Jonquiere, of making known to the premier of Quebec my views to the effect that municipalities, whose powers are derived exclusively from the provincial legislature, should first seek help from that body as being their immediate superior authority. As mayor of the most important city in the constituency of Lapointe, I offered the premier of Quebec my co-operation.
Though my offer dates from February 13 last, I have not yet had a reply. Our people, however, are still waiting, but there is a limit to their patience. The problem of unemployment must not become a political football. Provincial revenues, though smaller than those of the country as a whole, are nevertheless adequate, with the assistance currently given by the dominion government, who will increase it if necessary to provide jobs for our unemployed. Let us undertake the public works that are needed, those that were promised, for instance, during the last provincial elections in Quebec as well as those
The Budget-Mr. J. O. Gour for which $200 million were appropriated. That would greatly improve the situation.
I state without hesitation that the dominion government, having accomplished so much, must put forward a plan to alleviate unemployment. I must point out that the needs of my constituency are great. However, as the problem is one with which the government ought to deal with in part, I wish to state that my constituents have full confidence in our leaders and place all their trust in them. They know that if their efforts are supported as they should be by the provinces, for whom this is an imperative duty, there will be no undeserved hardship in a country so abundantly endowed by Providence.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I join with members who have spoken before me, and particularly the hon. member for Glengarry (Mr. Major), in sincerely regretting the unjustified rise in the price of grain since the first of January. It has put eastern farmers in a bad position. It has discouraged them because, with prices of feed as they are now, there is no more chance for a net profit. The federal government gave great help by way of subsidies of $6 for freight on feed, $3.50 per 100 pounds on bacon and three cents per pound on cheese, but all this help is lost now, so far as eastern farmers are concerned, in view of the prices they are obliged to pay for feed. They will quit feeding. They will stop raising cattle, pigs and chickens. Therefore there will be little demand for the grain of the western provinces. In the near future there will be a surplus of grain and they will be obliged to sell it at a very low price. The same thing happened many years ago when wheat was as high as $2 and $2.25 a bushel. We all remember what happened.
Therefore I think it is my duty to urge our good friends, the grain growers of the western provinces, not to create such a bad situation for their friends, the farmers of the east, who after all are their best customers, because in the near future they will need them to buy their grain and it will be too late. Today the bulk car price for No. 3 C.W. oats is $76 a ton at stations in eastern Ontario less a subsidy of $6 per ton. Barley is about the same. At the present time farmers, dealers and co-operatives refuse to buy. It will mean less bacon, less cheese, less chickens, and so on. The quoted price for grain on July 31 last was $15 less per ton. Why do we not have the July price today? If we did, our farmers would buy, the western farmers would get their money more quickly, and the eastern farmers would keep on producing the food. It would not create this misunderstanding between eastern farmers who need

The Budget-Mr. Bryce the grain and western farmers. The western farmer needs the eastern farmer to buy his grain. We need the best friendship we can possibly have. Two years ago I had the good fortune to go to all the western provinces, and all the people I met were very nice. It is true that some farmers were well off, while others were not in such good shape, but that is so at all times. They received us very nicely; but while our eastern farmers like the western people, we hope they will not try to get too much money right now. That will make for misunderstanding; and if the eastern farmers stop raising cattle and stop buying their feed grain, it will be just too bad. I hope they will not ask again for more money from the government or that they will not refuse to deliver their grain. Perhaps it is only natural to want to get another ten or twenty-five cents a bushel, but sometimes too much ambition is not good for you.
We hear a good deal of talk about discrimination with respect to income tax as between the western and eastern farmers. Well, in my riding there is a tax collector, just as there is everywhere else. I am sure the eastern people, farmers and others, who have any revenue are subject to the same income tax that is applied in other parts of Canada. The regulations and the law are the same. I pray God that my farmers will all have the means to pay income tax, because that would show that they had the revenue; and my farmers do not refuse to pay if they make enough. Therefore I hope there will be no more of this trying to set the people of the west against the people of the east, or race against race, and so on. We are all alike, and we should be developing the very best possible friendship between provinces, classes, religions and races. I hope things will continue as they are now, with the good government we are getting, and that the good understanding we have may increase. I am sure all those on this side of the house and indeed those on the opposition side as well have the same hope.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I repeat that something should be done by means of subsidies or in some other way to keep down these high prices, so that we may continue to be the best customers of the western farmers. We need the western people, as they need us. Therefore we should work together for the prosperity of this country.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I can assure the hon. member for Russell (Mr. Gour) that I am delighted with what he has said. I would remind him of the age-old
alliance between Scotland and France, and assure him that it still exists as between the east and the west in Canada. Let no Frenchman ever think western Canada is against him.
My hon. friend complains about the price he has to pay for his grain, and he blames the western farmer. It is not the western farmer who is to blame. I disagree with the hon. gentleman when he speaks of the good government we have. Why, it is the government we have that makes him pay these prices. They are not set by the western farmers. Certainly they want to get as much as they possibly can; but my hon. friend was one of the first to complain about the controls imposed by the government, though those controls enabled him to get his grain at a fair price. When we went back to the speculative system, call it private enterprise or what you like, we were robbed right and left. My hon. friend over here cannot produce eggs any more because costs are too high. The poultry farmer in Manitoba is up against the same thing today, and so is the man feeding steers. So we are all in the same boat; but if my hon. friend wants to correct the situation let him come over here and help me fight this thing, instead of sitting over there. As long as he is on that side of the house they will not listen to him; he will be only crying in the wilderness. We must have controls to see that the middleman does not get in and make more profit than the man who is feeding the hens, because that is what is happening. That is the man to blame, not the western farmer. We know you are one of our best markets, that you are going to buy the feed grains we cannot use ourselves. We are not going to make the price one you cannot pay, because if you do not get something for your labour certainly you will not continue to buy our grain, and we do not want that to happen.
Well, Mr. Speaker, there is a holiday feeling in the air tonight, and I should like to adjourn the debate so I may go further into these matters when we meet after Easter.
On motion of Mr. Bryce the debate was adjourned.
